instances.notes: Rule introduced in Brunei PDPO 2021 (Brunei, 2021-05-01).

instances.citation: Expanded Individual Rights — Third-Party Disclosure Scope
instances.notes: Both grant individuals the right to request disclosure of records relating to third-party provision of their data, but APPI expands the scope of disclosable records beyond Brunei's 12-month lookback period.

rule_text: You must implement measures to detect and prevent discriminatory outcomes from automated decision-making systems.
rule_text_technical: Controllers must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to detect and prevent discriminatory algorithmic outcomes resulting from automated processing, including profiling.

first_instance.law_name: Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (LOPDP, 2021) — Ecuador

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ecuador LOPDP 2021 (Ecuador, 2021-05-26).

Both address corrective action for discriminatory/biased algorithmic outcomes, but the ASEAN rule is a voluntary recommendation specifying concrete corrective measures (re-training, threshold adjustment) while the Ecuador rule is a binding mandate to implement detection and prevention measures.

instances.citation: Law No. 6563 & Law No. 6698 Amendment — Joint Liability (§ Affirmative Design Obligation)
instances.notes: Both require proactive design-level safeguards against harmful AI outputs, but the Ecuador rule focuses specifically on discriminatory outcomes from automated decision-making, whereas the Turkish bill imposes a broader affirmative design obligation covering harmful or infringing content generally.

rule_text: The SNPDP is empowered to issue binding regulations, guidelines, and codes of conduct applicable to data controllers and processors.
rule_text_technical: The Superintendencia de Protección de Datos Personales, as the independent supervisory authority, has the power to issue binding regulations, guidelines, and codes of conduct that are enforceable against controllers and processors operating within its jurisdiction.

first_instance.law_name: Ley Orgánica de Protección de Datos Personales (LOPDP, 2021) — Ecuador
first_instance.citation: LOPDP — SNPDP: Regulatory and Advisory Powers

instances.citation: LOPDP — SNPDP: Regulatory and Advisory Powers
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Ecuador LOPDP 2021 (Ecuador, 2021-05-26).

Both empower a national data protection authority to issue guidance to controllers and processors, but Sri Lanka's rule is narrowly scoped to issuing guidelines on the Data Protection Management Programme, while Ecuador's rule grants broader regulatory and advisory powers including binding regulations and codes of conduct.

rule_text: You must clearly disclose the limitations of the automated advisory service, including the types of financial situations the algorithm is not designed to address and circumstances where clients should seek human advice.
rule_text_technical: Licensees must clearly disclose the limitations of the automated advisory service, including: the types of financial situations or needs the algorithm is not designed to address; the scenarios in which the algorithm may produce suboptimal recommendations; and the circumstances in which clients should seek additional human advice.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

Both require disclosure of service scope and limitations to users, but the China rule is broader in scope (generative AI services, user groups, occasions, and lawful use guidance) while the Mauritius rule is sector-specific to algorithmic financial advisory limitations.

instances.citation: Risk Category: Confabulation / Disclosure to Users
instances.notes: Both call for disclosing system limitations to users to support informed reliance, but the Mauritius rule is a binding obligation scoped to automated financial advisory services, whereas this NIST guidance is a voluntary recommendation applicable to GenAI systems generally.

rule_text: You must clearly disclose all fees, charges, and any conflicts of interest that may affect the recommendations generated, including arrangements under which the algorithm may favor particular products.
rule_text_technical: Disclosures must include a clear explanation of all fees, charges, and any conflicts of interest that may affect the recommendations generated, including any arrangements under which the algorithm may favor particular products due to distribution agreements.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021
first_instance.citation: Disclosure Requirements § 4 (Fees and Conflicts of Interest)

instances.citation: Disclosure Requirements § 4 (Fees and Conflicts of Interest)
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

instances.citation: Proposed Rule 15l-2 / Advisers Act Rule — Core Requirement 2: Prohibition on Disclosure as Sole Remedy
instances.notes: The Mauritius rule treats disclosure of conflicts of interest as a sufficient compliance mechanism, while this SEC proposed rule explicitly rejects disclosure alone as adequate to satisfy conflict-of-interest obligations, making the two rules substantively opposed in their treatment of disclosure as a remedy.

rule_text: You must inform clients that all algorithmic models carry model risk, including the risk of incorrect or sub-optimal outputs due to flawed assumptions, data quality issues, or unanticipated market changes.
rule_text_technical: Licensees must inform clients that all algorithmic models carry model risk — the risk that the model may produce incorrect or sub-optimal outputs due to flawed assumptions, data quality issues, or changes in market conditions not anticipated by the model.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

Both require disclosure of the risk that AI/algorithmic models produce incorrect or misleading outputs, but the Mauritius rule is binding and sector-specific (financial advisory), while this NIST guidance is a voluntary, domain-agnostic recommendation covering GenAI confabulation broadly.

rule_text: You must conduct a rigorous client suitability assessment before providing robo-advisory services, gathering sufficient information about the client's financial situation, investment experience, risk tolerance, time horizon, and specific needs.
rule_text_technical: Licensees must conduct rigorous client suitability assessments before providing robo-advisory services. The assessment must gather sufficient information about the client's: financial situation and objectives; investment experience and knowledge; risk tolerance and capacity for loss; time horizon; and any specific financial needs or constraints.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

rule_text: You must designate a responsible individual — typically a senior compliance or technology officer — who is accountable for the ongoing operation and performance of the robo-advisory system.
rule_text_technical: Licensees must designate a responsible individual — typically a senior compliance or technology officer — who is accountable for the ongoing operation and performance of the robo-advisory system.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

Both rules require human oversight of AI systems, but the Shanghai rule is a high-level principle applying to government AI applications broadly (equity, transparency, oversight), while the Mauritius rule imposes a specific institutional accountability requirement (designated responsible individual); scope, specificity, and mechanism differ meaningfully.

Both address assigning defined roles and responsibilities for human oversight of AI systems, but the NIST rule is a voluntary recommendation about policy-level role differentiation across human-AI configurations, while the Mauritius rule is a binding requirement to designate a specific senior accountable individual.

Both require designation of a named responsible human professional accountable for AI oversight, but Utah's rule is scoped to high-risk interactions and frames the designee as a contact point for consumer questions/concerns, while the Mauritius rule designates a senior compliance or technology officer accountable for ongoing operation and performance of the AI system.

Both address human oversight in financial AI services, but Thailand's rule is specific to robo-advisory services and adds client suitability assessments, risk profiling, and algorithm disclosures, while the Mauritius rule focuses on designating a responsible individual accountable for ongoing operations.

rule_text: Before deploying a new algorithm or making a significant change to an existing algorithm, you must conduct internal validation and testing and must notify the FSC, which may require additional information or impose conditions prior to deployment.
rule_text_technical: Before deploying a new algorithm or making a significant change to an existing algorithm, licensees must conduct internal validation and testing and must notify the FSC. The FSC may require additional information or impose conditions before approving deployment of a materially changed algorithm.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021
first_instance.citation: Algorithm Transparency and Change Management § 2 (Approval for New Algorithms and Changes)

instances.citation: Algorithm Transparency and Change Management § 2 (Approval for New Algorithms and Changes)
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

Both require pre-deployment registration/notification with a regulator for AI/algorithmic services, but this rule is specific to deep synthesis providers with public opinion or social mobilization capacity and mandates a formal filing (备案) regime under Chinese internet regulation, whereas the Mauritius rule concerns internal validation and notification before algorithm deployment in financial services.

Both rules impose periodic reporting/notification obligations to a regulatory authority regarding AI-related implementations, but the Mauritius rule concerns pre-deployment notification of algorithm changes while this rule requires annual post-implementation reporting specifically on AI-generated content labelling compliance.

Both impose a pre-deployment verification/notification obligation related to algorithms or AI systems, but this rule requires the deployer to verify registration in a national registry rather than conduct internal validation and notify an authority.

Both rules require pre-deployment notification to a regulatory authority before operating an AI system, but Vietnam's rule applies specifically to medium-risk and high-risk AI systems notified through a designated single-window portal to the Ministry of Science and Technology, whereas Mauritius's rule focuses on algorithmic changes in the financial sector with internal validation requirements.

rule_text: You must ensure that the duty to provide suitable advice applies equally to algorithm-generated recommendations as to human-generated advice — automation does not diminish this obligation.
rule_text_technical: The duty to provide suitable advice applies equally to algorithm-generated recommendations as to human-generated advice. Licensees operating robo-advisory services remain subject to the full range of conduct of business obligations applicable under their license and under Mauritius financial services law, including fiduciary duties to act in clients' best interests.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021
first_instance.citation: Fiduciary Duties and Conduct Standards § 1 (Suitability of Advice)

instances.citation: Fiduciary Duties and Conduct Standards § 1 (Suitability of Advice)
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

rule_text: You must comply with applicable data protection obligations under the Mauritius Data Protection Act 2017 when operating robo-advisory platforms that process sensitive financial data.
rule_text_technical: Licensees must comply with applicable data protection obligations under the Mauritius Data Protection Act 2017, given that robo-advisory platforms process significant volumes of sensitive financial data.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021
first_instance.citation: Cybersecurity and Data Protection § 2 (Data Protection Compliance)

instances.citation: Cybersecurity and Data Protection § 2 (Data Protection Compliance)
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

Both impose a duty to ensure AI system deployment complies with data protection laws, but Peru's rule applies broadly to all AI deployers across sectors while Mauritius's rule is sector-specific to robo-advisory financial services platforms.

rule_text: Individuals have the right to request an explanation of why a particular AI-generated financial recommendation was made.
rule_text_technical: Consistent with Mauritius's obligations under the Data Protection Act 2017, clients receiving AI-generated financial advice have the right to request an explanation of why a particular recommendation was made.

first_instance.law_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules (Mauritius, 2021-06-01).

Both provide a right to explanation for AI-driven financial decisions, but the CFPB rule is a binding ECOA requirement specifically mandating specific reasons for adverse credit actions, while the Mauritius rule is a broader right to explanation for AI-generated financial recommendations with a different scope and obligation level.

Both rules concern the right to request an explanation of AI-assisted decisions, but the Argentine decree is a non-binding recommendation directed at public administration bodies for AI-assisted decisions broadly, while the Mauritius rule is a binding obligation in the financial services sector specifically.

rule_text: You must register with the PPC before transferring personal information to third parties via the opt-out mechanism; merely notifying the data subject is no longer sufficient.
rule_text_technical: Business operators wishing to transfer personal information to third parties under the opt-out framework must register with the PPC as a precondition to such transfer, replacing the prior regime under which notification to the data subject alone was sufficient.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

rule_text: You may use pseudonymously processed information for internal analytics and AI model training purposes, but you cannot provide it to third parties under ordinary circumstances.
rule_text_technical: Pseudonymously processed information — data processed so that individuals cannot be identified without reference to separately held additional information — may be retained and shared internally for analytics and research, including AI development and testing, but is prohibited from provision to third parties under ordinary circumstances.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

Both Korea PIPA 2023 and Japan APPI 2022 permit use of pseudonymous/pseudonymously processed information for research and analytics without consent, but PIPA 2023 explicitly extends permitted purposes to public records preservation and omits the third-party transfer restriction that is central to the Japanese rule.

rule_text: You must comply with data subject rights requests submitted electronically.
rule_text_technical: Business operators are obligated to accept and comply with requests from data subjects exercising their personal data rights when those requests are submitted through electronic means.

first_instance.law_name: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) — 2022 Amendments (Act No. 57 of 2003, as amended by Act No. 77 of 2021, in force June 2022)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Japan APPI (2022 Amendments) (Japan, 2021-06-04).

Both rules address the ability to submit data subject rights requests in electronic/technological format, but Quebec's rule is permissive (requests 'may' be in writing and submitted technologically) whereas Japan's APPI imposes a compliance obligation on the controller to accept electronic submissions.

Both rules relate to compliance with Japan's APPI and personal data subject rights, but this guideline is a soft-law recommendation focused on purpose limitation and privacy-by-design for AI systems, whereas the existing APPI rule concerns the binding obligation to accept electronically submitted data subject rights requests.

rule_text: You cannot infringe upon natural persons' personal information rights and interests.
rule_text_technical: No organization or individual may infringe upon natural persons' personal information rights and interests, which receive legal protection.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China PIPL (AI provisions) (China, 2021-08-20).

Both rules operate within China's AI/data legal framework and require compliance with overlapping Chinese laws, but this rule specifically mandates compliance with multiple named statutes (Cybersecurity Law, Data Security Law, PIPL) in the context of generative AI services, while the existing rule is a standalone personal information rights protection obligation.

rule_text: You cannot illegally collect, use, process, transmit, sell, buy, provide, or disclose other persons' personal information, or engage in personal information handling activities that harm national security or the public interest.
rule_text_technical: No organization or individual may illegally collect, use, process, or transmit other persons' personal information, or illegally sell, buy, provide, or disclose other persons' personal information, or engage in personal information handling activities harming national security or the public interest.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China PIPL (AI provisions) (China, 2021-08-20).

Both prohibit illegal manipulation of personal information and accounts, but this rule is specifically targeted at algorithmic misuse for fake accounts, artificial engagement, and content manipulation, whereas the PIPL rule broadly prohibits illegal collection, use, and trading of personal information.

Both are Chinese binding regulations prohibiting unlawful production and dissemination of information, but this rule is narrower in scope (deep synthesis/AI-generated content specifically) whereas PIPL Art. 10 addresses personal information processing broadly.

Both are Chinese binding instruments protecting individuals' lawful rights (including personal information and dignity), but this rule is generative-AI-specific and explicitly covers image, reputation, and psychological well-being, whereas PIPL focuses on personal information processing.

Both prohibit covert or unlawful collection and processing of personal information without consent, but this rule is specific to facial recognition technology and covert tracking/matching, whereas the PIPL rule covers all personal information broadly.

Both prohibit unlawful exploitation of systems/information to harm others' rights, but the Vietnam rule is AI-specific and broader in framing 'exploit or misappropriate AI systems', whereas the Chinese rule targets personal information processing specifically.

rule_text: You must obtain the individual's consent again if there is any change in the purpose, method, or categories of personal information handled.
rule_text_technical: Where a change occurs in the purpose of personal information handling, the handling method, or the categories of handled personal information, the individual's consent shall be obtained again.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China PIPL (AI provisions) (China, 2021-08-20).

Both rules address the need for renewed consent or disclosure when data is used for a new purpose beyond its original collection, but the Chinese rule requires obtaining consent again for any change in purpose, while the FTC rule focuses specifically on AI training and requires only 'adequate disclosure or consent,' setting a lower or alternative threshold.

instances.citation: Key Provisions § 2 (Consent Requirement — Creation vs. Distribution)
instances.notes: Both rules address the granularity and separateness of consent for distinct purposes, but Alabama HB 161 specifically targets AI-generated intimate imagery and distinguishes creation consent from distribution consent, whereas China PIPL Art. 14-2 addresses re-consent when the purpose or method of personal information handling changes.

Both rules require fresh consent when personal data is repurposed beyond its original collection purpose, but this soft-law guidance specifically targets AI training contexts and allows a 'new lawful basis' as an alternative, whereas the PIPL binding rule focuses on changes in purpose, method, or categories requiring re-consent.

rule_text: You must notify individuals of any changes to the matters previously disclosed to them.
rule_text_technical: Where a change occurs in the matters provided in the previous paragraph, individuals shall be notified about the change.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China PIPL (AI provisions) (China, 2021-08-20).

Both require notifying individuals of material changes to previously disclosed processing activities, but the China PIPL rule is a binding legal mandate while this HK guidance is a voluntary recommendation, and the HK rule is specifically scoped to AI systems processing personal data.

rule_text: Where the highest authority person does not personally exercise those functions, they must still facilitate the exercise of those functions by the delegate.
rule_text_technical: Where the person exercising the highest authority within a public body does not exercise those functions himself, he must see to it that such exercise is facilitated.

first_instance.law_name: An Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information (SQ 2021, c 25)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Quebec Law 25 (Privacy Modernization Act) (Quebec, 2021-09-22).

rule_text: You must notify the Commission in writing as soon as possible of the title, contact information, and starting date of the person exercising the functions of person in charge of access to documents and person in charge of the protection of personal information.
rule_text_technical: The public body must, as soon as possible, notify the Commission in writing of the title, contact information and starting date of the person who exercises the function of person in charge of access to documents and those of the person who exercises the function of person in charge of the protection of personal information.

first_instance.law_name: An Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information (SQ 2021, c 25)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Quebec Law 25 (Privacy Modernization Act) (Quebec, 2021-09-22).

Both rules require notifying a supervisory authority of a DPO appointment, but the Quebec rule specifies the content of the notification (title, contact info, start date) while the Malaysian rule focuses on the manner and form determined by the Commissioner, and the Malaysian rule is framed as a controller obligation under a binding statute rather than a general notification requirement.

rule_text: Within a public body, you must establish a committee on access to information and the protection of personal information to support the body in fulfilling its responsibilities and obligations under the Act.
rule_text_technical: Within a public body, a committee on access to information and the protection of personal information is responsible for supporting the body in the exercise of its responsibilities and the performance of its obligations under this Act, and shall also exercise the functions entrusted to it by this Act.

first_instance.law_name: An Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information (SQ 2021, c 25)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Quebec Law 25 (Privacy Modernization Act) (Quebec, 2021-09-22).

Both require establishing an internal committee responsible for overseeing a specific compliance domain, but this rule targets scientific and technological ethics review rather than access to information and personal data protection within public bodies.

rule_text: The committee must be under the responsibility of the highest authority (or deputy minister / director general as applicable) and must include the person in charge of access to documents, the person in charge of the protection of personal information, and any other person whose expertise is required.
rule_text_technical: The committee is under the responsibility of the person exercising the highest authority within the public body or, in the case of a government department, of the deputy minister and, in the case of a municipality, a professional order or a school board, of the director general; it is composed of the person in charge of access to documents, the person in charge of the protection of personal information and any other person whose expertise is required, including, if applicable, the person responsible for information security and the person responsible for document management.

first_instance.law_name: An Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information (SQ 2021, c 25)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Quebec Law 25 (Privacy Modernization Act) (Quebec, 2021-09-22).

rule_text: A government regulation may exempt a public body from the obligation to establish such a committee or modify a body's obligations according to defined criteria.
rule_text_technical: A government regulation may exempt a public body from the obligation to establish such a committee or modify a body's obligations according to criteria it defines.

first_instance.law_name: An Act to modernize legislative provisions as regards the protection of personal information (SQ 2021, c 25)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Quebec Law 25 (Privacy Modernization Act) (Quebec, 2021-09-22).

rule_text: As a data processor, you may only process personal data on documented instructions from the data controller.
rule_text_technical: Processors may only act on documented instructions from the data controller when processing personal data; processing outside such instructions is prohibited.

first_instance.law_name: Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 Regarding the Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in UAE PDPL (Federal Decree-Law 45/2021) (United Arab Emirates, 2021-09-26).

instances.citation: Jordan PDPL 2023 — Data Processor Agreements: Instruction Requirement
instances.notes: Both rules require processors to act only on documented instructions from the controller and prohibit independent processing, drafted differently but substantively equivalent.

instances.citation: Art. 1 / Processor Obligation — Acting on Instructions
instances.notes: Both independently establish that a data processor may only process personal data on documented instructions from the data controller, drafted differently but substantively equivalent.

Both restrict use to specified purposes and conditions set by another party, but Peru's rule concerns deployers of high-risk AI systems following provider specifications, while the UAE rule concerns data processors following controller instructions.

rule_text: You must implement data protection principles from the design stage of new systems and processes, and ensure that by default only personal data necessary for each specific purpose is processed.
rule_text_technical: Controllers are required to implement data protection principles from the design stage of new systems and processes (privacy by design) and to ensure that, by default, only personal data necessary for each specific processing purpose is processed (privacy by default).

first_instance.law_name: Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 Regarding the Protection of Personal Data

instances.notes: Rule introduced in UAE PDPL (Federal Decree-Law 45/2021) (United Arab Emirates, 2021-09-26).

Both require compliance with data protection laws and privacy-by-design principles, but Peru's rule applies specifically to AI systems while the UAE rule applies broadly to new systems and processes; also Peru's is an AI-specific statute while UAE's is a general data protection law.

Both recommend embedding privacy by design from the earliest development stages, but the existing rule is from a binding law while this is voluntary guidance specifically targeting AI development contexts.

Both require privacy by design in system development, but the UAE rule is a binding legal mandate for data protection generally while this is a voluntary AI-specific recommendation under Australian law.
Both rules require that by default only necessary personal data is processed; Chile's rule is independently drafted and standalone while the UAE rule bundles it with design requirements.

rule_text: Where a DPIA reveals a high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, you must consult with the NCSA before commencing the processing.
rule_text_technical: Where a data protection impact assessment indicates that the processing would result in a high residual risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk, the controller must consult the NCSA prior to commencing the processing.

first_instance.law_name: Law N° 058/2021 of 13/10/2021 Relating to the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy in Rwanda

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Rwanda Data Protection and Privacy Law 2021 (Rwanda, 2021-10-13).

Both involve evaluating whether residual negative risk exceeds an acceptable threshold, but the Rwanda DPA rule is a binding requirement to consult a regulator when high residual risk remains, while the NIST rule is a voluntary recommendation to evaluate and ensure residual risk stays within tolerance.

Both require prior consultation with a supervisory authority when a DPIA reveals high residual risk, but Pakistan specifies the PDPA Authority while Rwanda specifies the NCSA, and the drafting is independent.

Both rules require prior consultation with the national data protection authority when a DPIA reveals high residual risk that cannot be mitigated, but Ethiopia refers to the EDPA while Rwanda refers to the NCSA, and Ethiopia additionally specifies the condition 'by the controller alone'; same substantive obligation, independently drafted.

rule_text: You may benefit from simplified data transfer procedures when transferring personal data to countries party to regional agreements, such as those under the EAC or AfCFTA, that provide equivalent data protection.
rule_text_technical: In recognition of Rwanda's regional integration commitments under the East African Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area, the Law provides for simplified transfer procedures in respect of transfers to countries that are party to relevant regional agreements providing equivalent data protection standards.

first_instance.law_name: Law N° 058/2021 of 13/10/2021 Relating to the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy in Rwanda

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Rwanda Data Protection and Privacy Law 2021 (Rwanda, 2021-10-13).

rule_text: You must ensure that any automated employment decision tool (AEDT) used to screen candidates or employees in New York City has been subject to a bias audit conducted by an independent auditor before the tool is used.
rule_text_technical: Employers and employment agencies must not use an automated employment decision tool to screen a candidate for employment or an employee for a promotion unless the tool has been the subject of a bias audit conducted by an independent auditor prior to such use.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

rule_text: You must use an auditor who is not involved in using or developing the AEDT to conduct the required bias audit.
rule_text_technical: The bias audit required under this subchapter must be conducted by an independent auditor, defined as a person or group that is not involved in using or developing the AEDT that is responsible for conducting such audit.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

rule_text: You must use historical data when conducting a bias audit of an AEDT, including data collected from prior use of the tool by employers or vendors.
rule_text_technical: The bias audit must be conducted using historical data, which may include data collected by the vendor from employers on applicants selected through the AEDT or historical data on scores or outcomes generated by the tool for each relevant category.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

rule_text: You must calculate an impact ratio as part of the bias audit to assess whether the AEDT has an adverse impact on protected categories, including sex, race/ethnicity, and intersectional categories.
rule_text_technical: The bias audit must include calculation of an impact ratio for sex categories, race/ethnicity categories, and intersectional categories of sex and race/ethnicity, comparing selection or scoring rates of each category against the most-selected or highest-scoring category.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

Both address adverse impact on protected groups in employment selection, but the EEOC rule imposes a direct prohibition with a business necessity/job-relatedness justification standard under Title VII/UGESP, while NYC LL144 requires a quantitative bias audit and impact ratio calculation as a compliance mechanism.

Both address preventing discriminatory outcomes of AI systems against protected classes in employment, but NYC LL144 prescribes a specific impact-ratio audit methodology, whereas the Illinois provision is a broader non-discrimination mandate without specifying a technical measurement standard.

rule_text: You must publish the results of the bias audit on your website in a clear and conspicuous manner, including the date of the audit, the source and date range of data used, and the impact ratios calculated.
rule_text_technical: Employers and employment agencies must publish on their website, in a clear and conspicuous manner, the results of the most recent bias audit of any AEDT used, including: the date the bias audit was conducted; the name of the independent auditor; the source and date range of the data used; the number of individuals in each category; and the impact ratios for each category examined.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

rule_text: You must retain published bias audit results on your website for at least six months after you stop using the AEDT to which the results apply.
rule_text_technical: The published bias audit results must remain publicly available on the employer's or employment agency's website for a period of no less than six months after the employer or employment agency ceases use of the AEDT to which those results pertain.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

rule_text: You must provide notice on the careers or jobs section of your website in a clear and conspicuous manner at least 10 business days before using an AEDT to screen a candidate for employment who resides in New York City.
rule_text_technical: For the purpose of compliance with § 20-871(b)(1) and (2) of the Code, an employer or employment agency may provide notice to a candidate for employment who resides in the city by including notice on the careers or jobs section of its website in a clear and conspicuous manner at least 10 business days prior to use of an AEDT.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

Both require disclosure/notice to applicants and employees when AI or automated decision-making tools are used in employment decisions, but NYC LL144 is more specific (requires 10-business-day advance notice, website posting, and applies to AEDTs in NYC), while the Illinois IHRA amendment is a broader statewide anti-discrimination framework requiring general transparency about AI use in employment without the same procedural specificity.

rule_text: You may alternatively provide notice to candidates by including the required information in the job posting or by notifying the candidate directly at least 10 business days before using the AEDT.
rule_text_technical: An employer or employment agency may alternatively satisfy the notice requirement by including notice in the job posting for the position for which the AEDT will be used, or by providing direct written notice to the candidate at least 10 business days prior to use of the AEDT.

rule_text: You must provide notice to current employees who reside in New York City at least 10 business days before using an AEDT to assess them for a promotion.
rule_text_technical: For the purpose of compliance with § 20-871(b)(2) of the Code, an employer or employment agency must provide notice to a current employee who resides in the city at least 10 business days prior to use of an AEDT in connection with assessing that employee for a promotion.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

Both require disclosure to employees and job applicants when automated decision-making tools are used in employment contexts, but NYC LL 144 specifies a 10-business-day advance notice requirement and is limited to AEDT tools for hiring/promotion, while the Illinois amendment is broader in scope (covering AI generally in employment decisions) and does not specify the same timing or procedural detail.

rule_text: The notice provided to candidates and employees must include instructions for how to request an alternative selection process or accommodation.
rule_text_technical: The notice required by § 20-871(b)(1) of the Code must include instructions for how to request an alternative selection process or accommodation, in addition to other required content elements.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

rule_text: You are not required to provide an alternative selection process or accommodation to candidates or employees who request one in response to the required notice.
rule_text_technical: Nothing in this subchapter requires an employer or employment agency to provide an alternative selection process or accommodation in response to a request made by a candidate or employee pursuant to the notice requirements of § 5-303.

first_instance.citation: § 5-303(e) (No Obligation to Provide Alternative Selection Process)

instances.citation: § 5-303(e) (No Obligation to Provide Alternative Selection Process)

rule_text: You cannot use an AEDT to screen a candidate for employment or an employee for a promotion unless a valid bias audit has been completed and the required notice has been provided.
rule_text_technical: It shall be unlawful for an employer or employment agency to use an automated employment decision tool to screen a candidate for employment or an employee for a promotion where the employer or employment agency has not: (1) obtained a bias audit of the tool conducted by an independent auditor; and (2) provided notice to candidates and employees in accordance with the requirements of this subchapter.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law
first_instance.citation: § 20-871(b)(1)–(2) (Code — Prohibition Without Bias Audit and Notice)

instances.citation: § 20-871(b)(1)–(2) (Code — Prohibition Without Bias Audit and Notice)
instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

Both rules impose mandatory requirements on employers using AI in employment decisions, but NYC LL144 focuses specifically on bias audits and screening prohibitions for AEDTs, while Utah SB226 imposes broader high-risk AI disclosure and oversight requirements covering hiring recommendations and performance evaluations without a bias audit mechanism.

Both rules address AI/automated tools in employment decisions (recruitment screening, candidate evaluation), but NYC LL144 focuses on prohibiting use without a completed bias audit, while Peru's Art. 5(c) classifies such systems as high-risk without specifying a bias audit mechanism, representing a different regulatory approach (risk classification vs. audit-gated prohibition).

Both prohibit discriminatory use of AI/automated tools in employment decisions, but NYC LL144 focuses on mandatory bias audits and screening procedures with specific procedural requirements, while the Illinois amendment broadly prohibits discriminatory outcomes under human rights law without mandating a specific audit mechanism.

rule_text: You must ensure the bias audit of an AEDT was conducted no more than one year before the date the tool is used.
rule_text_technical: An employer or employment agency must not use an AEDT unless the bias audit relied upon was conducted within one year prior to the date of use, ensuring that audit results remain current and applicable to the tool as deployed.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

rule_text: You must publish a summary of the methodology used by the independent auditor when publishing bias audit results.
rule_text_technical: The published bias audit results must include a description of the bias audit's methodology, including the statistical measures used to calculate adverse impact, sufficient to allow meaningful evaluation of the audit's scope and approach.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

Both address algorithmic bias, but the Tunisia rule is a voluntary recommendation to establish a framework for identifying and addressing algorithmic bias broadly, while the NYC rule is a binding requirement to publish audit methodology summaries for automated employment decision tools specifically.

Both rules require disclosure of audit-related information to the public, but NYC LL144 requires publishing audit methodology summaries for bias audits of automated employment decision tools, while this California rule requires disclosing whether an audit under a specific statutory provision has been conducted and its results, applying to a broader data protection context with a future effective date of 2029.

rule_text: The notice and bias audit requirements apply when screening candidates for employment or employees for promotion who reside in New York City.
rule_text_technical: The obligations imposed under this subchapter apply with respect to candidates for employment who reside in New York City and employees who reside in New York City, limiting the jurisdictional scope of the notice and audit requirements to New York City residents.

first_instance.law_name: New York City Automated Employment Decision Tools Law

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NYC Local Law 144 (AEDT) (New York City, 2021-11-10).

instances.citation: Public Act 103-0804 — Scope: Hiring and Employment
instances.notes: Both rules define the scope of AI employment obligations across stages of hiring and employment, but the Illinois rule applies state-wide to all stages of hiring and employment under a non-discrimination framework, whereas NYC Local Law 144 focuses on screening candidates/employees for hiring and promotion within New York City with a bias audit mechanism.

rule_text: Organizations should not use AI in ways that undermine peaceful, just, and interconnected societies, and should work to prevent the misuse of AI to spread hate speech, propaganda, or disinformation.
rule_text_technical: AI should not be used in a way that undermines peaceful, just, and interconnected societies. AI actors should work to prevent the misuse of AI to spread hate speech, propaganda, or disinformation that could be harmful to societies. AI systems should promote justice, inclusion, solidarity, and democratic participation.

first_instance.law_name: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
first_instance.citation: Part IV, Value 2 (Living in Peaceful, Just, and Interconnected Societies)

instances.citation: Part IV, Value 2 (Living in Peaceful, Just, and Interconnected Societies)
instances.notes: Rule introduced in UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation (UNESCO, 2021-11-23).

Both prohibit use of AI/algorithmic systems in ways that undermine societal order and harm rights, but the Chinese rule is a binding legal obligation focused on national security and economic order, whereas the UNESCO rule is a voluntary recommendation framed around peaceful societies.

Both prohibit using AI to spread false or harmful information (fake news/disinformation), but this rule is a binding Chinese regulation specifically targeting deep synthesis services with a news-reprinting disclosure obligation, whereas the UNESCO rule is a voluntary recommendation with broader societal scope.

Both are voluntary/soft-law instruments recommending against harmful AI misuse, but the ASEAN rule focuses specifically on circumventing legal obligations and deceptive manipulation of individuals, while the UNESCO rule addresses undermining peaceful societies and spreading harmful content, making them conceptually overlapping but substantively distinct in focus.

Both rules address constraining AI applications that could harm individuals through surveillance or profiling, but the China 2023 rule imposes a binding ethics review obligation specifically for social monitoring, tracking, and behavioral analysis, whereas the UNESCO recommendation is a voluntary instrument with broader framing around preventing AI misuse in societies.

Both prohibit AI-generated content that undermines societal peace and spreads harmful ideologies, but the Chinese binding regulation specifies concrete prohibited categories (subversion of sovereignty, terrorism, ethnic hatred) while the UNESCO recommendation is voluntary and broader in framing.

Both prohibit AI misuse that undermines individuals or society through manipulation, but Peru's rule is a binding legal prohibition specifically targeting subliminal/deceptive techniques against individual interests without consent, whereas the UNESCO rule is a voluntary recommendation focused on societal-level peaceful coexistence.

Both prohibit using AI in ways that undermine societal stability and prevent spread of harmful content, but the Beijing rule is a binding regulation with a specific socialist-values framing and state-power protection focus, whereas the UNESCO rule is a voluntary recommendation with a broader peaceful-societies orientation.

instances.citation: Section IV, Prohibition on Harmful Applications
instances.notes: Both are voluntary instruments prohibiting AI uses that violate human rights or undermine peaceful societies, but the UN resolution explicitly grounds the prohibition in international human rights law and international humanitarian law, while the UNESCO recommendation focuses more broadly on preventing misuse to spread harm.

Both instruments prohibit using AI in ways that undermine democratic institutions and peaceful societies, but the CoE Framework Convention focuses specifically on democratic integrity, independence, and effectiveness, while the UNESCO Recommendation addresses broader peaceful and just societies; additionally, the CoE instrument is a binding treaty whereas UNESCO's is voluntary, though both are treated here as soft law comparators given the CoE convention's framework nature.

Both recommend AI be used for societal benefit and human dignity, but the Argentine decree focuses on individual/societal benefit framing while the UNESCO rule centers on peaceful and just societies; both are soft-law instruments with different scope and phrasing.

Both address prohibitions on inciting enmity or hatred against groups, but the Singapore rule is a binding statutory prohibition on online material inciting hostility against groups in Singapore, while the UNESCO rule is a non-binding recommendation against misuse of AI to spread hatred more broadly.

rule_text: Organizations should implement security measures to protect the integrity of AI systems against adversarial attacks, interference, and manipulation, encompassing both the AI systems and the data and infrastructure on which they rely.
rule_text_technical: AI actors must work to ensure the integrity of AI systems themselves against adversarial attacks, interference, and manipulation. Security measures should encompass not only the AI systems but also the data and infrastructure on which they rely.

first_instance.law_name: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

instances.notes: Rule introduced in UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation (UNESCO, 2021-11-23).

Both address AI system security and resilience, but NIST's rule is specifically about evaluation and documentation of security/resilience, while the UNESCO rule focuses on implementing protective security measures against adversarial attacks; both are voluntary instruments.

Both recommend security controls (physical, cyber, insider threats) to protect AI system integrity, but the G7 rule is voluntary soft law focused on advanced AI developers while the UNESCO recommendation has broader scope; both are non-binding but drafted independently with different framing.

Both address cybersecurity/security measures to protect AI systems against adversarial manipulation and unauthorized interference, but the Peru rule is a binding legal requirement scoped to high-risk AI systems, while the UNESCO rule is a voluntary recommendation with broader organizational scope.

instances.citation: Appendix A – Risk Category: AI Design and Implementation Failures
instances.notes: Both recommend integrating safety and security as core design considerations for AI systems, but this DHS rule explicitly frames safety and security as non-afterthoughts in a critical infrastructure context, while the UNESCO recommendation focuses more broadly on protecting integrity against adversarial attacks.

rule_text: Member States should establish data protection governance procedures through a multilateral approach, supported by legal systems, to achieve global data protection standards.
rule_text_technical: In order to establish global data protection standards and governance procedures, supported by legal systems, a multilateral approach is recommended. The principles and regulations governing the harvesting, use and dissemination of personal data, together with the exercise of rights by data subjects, must be assimilated within local data protection laws and any accompanying mechanisms.

first_instance.law_name: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
first_instance.citation: Part V, Principle 3 (Right to Privacy and Data Protection)

instances.citation: Part V, Principle 3 (Right to Privacy and Data Protection)
instances.notes: Rule introduced in UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation (UNESCO, 2021-11-23).

Both assign UNESCO a governance role on AI ethics and support for Member States, but this UN rule expands the mandate to include AI education and cultural diversity aspects, while the UNESCO recommendation focuses specifically on data protection governance.

instances.citation: Key Provisions § AI for Public Good — UNESCO Body
instances.notes: Both reference UNESCO as a venue for international AI governance cooperation, but this rule proposes a specific new international AI research body under UNESCO, whereas the UNESCO recommendation concerns data protection governance procedures via a multilateral approach.

rule_text: If you operate critical national information infrastructure, you must comply with mandated security standards.
rule_text_technical: Operators of designated critical national information infrastructure sectors are subject to a binding obligation to comply with mandated security standards as established under the Act.

first_instance.citation: Part II — Critical Infrastructure Protection (Security Standards)

instances.citation: Part II — Critical Infrastructure Protection (Security Standards)
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Zimbabwe Cybersecurity and Data Protection Act 2021 (Zimbabwe, 2021-12-13).

Both require heightened governance practices for AI or technology in critical infrastructure, but the Zimbabwe rule is a binding cybersecurity mandate while this is a voluntary AI governance recommendation.

instances.citation: Cybersecurity Act B.E. 2562 (CII Operators — Security Requirements)
instances.notes: Both require critical information infrastructure operators to comply with security requirements, but the Thailand rule is more specific in mandating risk assessments, security monitoring, and incident response specifically for AI system deployments.

instances.citation: Appendix A – Risk Category: Attacks on AI
instances.notes: Both address security of AI systems supporting critical infrastructure, but the DHS rule is voluntary guidance covering API and model endpoint security, while the Zimbabwe rule is a binding mandate requiring compliance with mandated security standards for critical national information infrastructure.

rule_text: You cannot access a computer system without authorization.
rule_text_technical: Unauthorized access to computer systems is a criminal offense under the Act, carrying prescribed criminal penalties.

rule_text: You cannot interfere with or sabotage computer systems or data.
rule_text_technical: System interference and sabotage, including unauthorized interference with the operation of computer systems or data, constitutes a criminal offense under the Act.

rule_text_technical: Computer fraud and forgery using computer systems or data are criminal offenses under the Act, subject to prescribed penalties.

rule_text: You must orient your algorithmic recommendation services toward mainstream values, optimize recommendation mechanisms, and actively transmit positive energy.
rule_text_technical: Algorithmic recommendation service providers shall persist in being oriented towards mainstream values, optimize mechanisms for algorithmic recommendation services, actively transmit positive energy, and promote the uplifting use of algorithms.

first_instance.law_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

Both rules require AI/algorithmic service providers to align their services with laws, social ethics, and mainstream/correct values, but this rule is specific to deep synthesis services while the existing rule addresses algorithmic recommendation mechanisms.

Both rules impose conduct obligations on AI service providers under Chinese law, but this rule specifically addresses intellectual property rights, commercial ethics, and anti-monopoly concerns in the context of generative AI, whereas the existing rule focuses on algorithmic recommendation services and mainstream value orientation.

Both rules require AI governance measures consistent with national requirements, but Guangdong's rule focuses on establishing provincial safety and governance standards and guidelines, while China's algorithmic recommendation rule specifically addresses mainstream value orientation in recommendation services.

rule_text: You must maintain a pool of characteristics to identify illegal and negative content, and any algorithmically generated or synthesized information that is not conspicuously labeled must be labeled before further transmission.
rule_text_technical: Providers of algorithmic recommendation services shall strengthen information security management, establish and complete a pool of characteristics used to identify illegal and negative content, and improve standards, rules, and procedures for inclusion in the pool. Where algorithmically generated or synthesized information is discovered without a conspicuous label, transmission may continue only after making a conspicuous label.

first_instance.law_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

Both address the need to identify and mitigate risks from algorithmically generated disinformation and synthetic content, but the NIST rule is a voluntary recommendation focused on organizational risk assessment broadly, while the Chinese rule is a binding mandate requiring maintenance of a specific content-identification pool.

Both require operators to use technical measures to identify AI-generated/synthesized illegal content, but this rule is framed as a Cybersecurity Law network operator obligation focused on cybersecurity threats, whereas the existing rule targets algorithmic recommendation service providers maintaining pools of characteristics for illegal and negative content.

rule_text: You must immediately stop transmission of unlawful information, take steps to eliminate or address it, preserve records, and report to cybersecurity and informatization departments and relevant authorities; negative information must be addressed per internet content ecology regulations.
rule_text_technical: Where unlawful information is discovered, providers shall immediately stop transmission, employ measures to eliminate or otherwise address it, stop the spread of the information, store relevant records, and report to the cybersecurity and informatization departments and relevant departments. Where negative information is discovered, it shall be addressed in accordance with the relevant provisions on the management of the internet information content ecology.

first_instance.law_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

The rule is functionally near-identical to the Algorithm Recommendation regulation's Art. 9(2), requiring the same sequence of actions upon discovering illegal information: address it, preserve records, and report to telecommunications/cybersecurity authorities.

Both rules require providers to take action against illegal content/activities by users of AI services, but the Algorithm Recommendation rule focuses on stopping transmission and reporting to authorities, while this rule focuses on graduated user-facing sanctions (warnings, function limits, account suspension/termination) specific to generative AI services.

Both require rapid removal of unlawful content (24 hours here vs. immediate in China) and attach penalties, but this rule is specific to child pornography with criminal sanctions (1 year imprisonment), while the Chinese rule covers unlawful information generally with reporting obligations.

rule_text: You must strengthen user modeling and tag management, establish rules for recording user interests, and cannot use unlawful or negative information keywords as user interest records or tags for pushing information.
rule_text_technical: Providers of algorithmic recommendation services shall strengthen the management of user modeling and user tags, improving rules for recording the interests of user models and rules for managing user tags; keywords that are unlawful or negative information must not be used as recorded user interests or user tags used to push information.

first_instance.law_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

rule_text: You are encouraged to use strategies such as deduplication and fragmentation and to optimize the transparency and explainability of search, sorting, selection, pushing, and display rules to avoid negative impacts on users and prevent disputes.
rule_text_technical: Providers of algorithmic recommendation services are encouraged to comprehensively use strategies such as eliminating duplicate content and fragmentation and intervention, and optimize the transparency and explainability of rules for searches, sorting, selections, pushing, and displays, to avoid producing a negative impact on users, and to prevent and reduce contention and disputes.

first_instance.law_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

Both address transparency and explainability of AI/algorithmic outputs, but NIST AI RMF is a voluntary framework focused on model documentation and contextual interpretation, while the Chinese regulation is a binding instrument encouraging transparency in recommendation algorithms with a narrower sectoral scope.

rule_text: You cannot generate or synthesize fake news or transmit news from unauthorized units; if you provide internet news information services, you must obtain the required permit and conduct services lawfully.
rule_text_technical: Where providers of algorithmic recommendation services provide Internet news information services, they shall obtain Internet news information service permits in accordance with law, regulate the carrying out of Internet news information collection, publication, forwarding, and transmission platform services, and must not generate or synthesize fake news information or transmit news information from units not within the scope provided by the state.

first_instance.law_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

rule_text: You cannot use algorithms to unreasonably restrict other internet information service providers or undermine their normal operations in a manner constituting monopoly or unfair competition.
rule_text_technical: Providers of algorithmic recommendation services must not use algorithms to unreasonably restrict other internet information service providers, or to obstruct and undermine the normal operation of the internet information services they lawfully provide, implementing a monopoly or unfair competition.

first_instance.law_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

Both rules prohibit anticompetitive use of algorithms to restrain trade or harm competitors, but the California rule specifically targets 'common pricing algorithms' used in cartel-like price-fixing conspiracies under antitrust law, while the Chinese rule focuses on algorithms that restrict other internet service providers' operations.

rule_text: When providing services to minors, you must fulfill legal obligations to protect minors online and facilitate minors' access to beneficial and healthy information through age-appropriate modes and services.
rule_text_technical: Where providers of algorithmic recommendation services provide services to minors, they shall perform obligations to protect minors online in accordance with law, and facilitate minors obtaining beneficial and healthy information through methods such as having modes appropriate for use by minors and providing services suited to the characteristics of minors.

first_instance.law_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

rule_text: When providing services to seniors, you must safeguard their lawful rights and interests, provide smart services suited to their needs in travel, medical care, spending, and affairs, monitor for telecom fraud, and facilitate seniors' safe use of algorithmic recommendation services.
rule_text_technical: When providers of algorithmic recommendation services provide seniors with services, they shall safeguard the rights and interests lawfully enjoyed by seniors, fully consider the needs of seniors in travel, seeking medical care, spending, and handling affairs; provide smart services suited to seniors in accordance with relevant state provisions; carry out monitoring, recognition, and handling of information involving telecommunication network fraud, and facilitate seniors' safe use of algorithmic recommendation services.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in China Algorithm Recommendations Regulation (China, 2021-12-31).

rule_text: You may process personal data where processing is necessary for the performance of a task in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority.
rule_text_technical: Processing is lawful where it is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller.

first_instance.citation: Lawful Bases for Processing — Public Interest

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Oman PDPL 2022 (Oman, 2022-02-09).

instances.citation: Jordan PDPL 2023 — Lawful Bases for Processing: Public Interest / Official Authority
instances.notes: Both permit processing necessary for public interest tasks or the exercise of official authority, independently drafted with equivalent substance.

rule_text: You must obtain specific authorization before deploying biometric identification systems in public or employment contexts.
rule_text_technical: Biometric identification systems deployed in public or employment contexts require specific authorization.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Law — Royal Decree No. 6/2022 (Oman)
first_instance.citation: Special Categories of Sensitive Data — Biometric Identification Systems

instances.citation: Special Categories of Sensitive Data — Biometric Identification Systems
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Oman PDPL 2022 (Oman, 2022-02-09).

Both require prior authorization before deploying biometric identification systems in public contexts, but Peru's rule is more specific, limiting use to State actors with prior judicial authorization and enumerating exhaustive permitted purposes (fugitives, missing persons, terrorism prevention).

Both require authorization or consent before deploying biometric identification systems in employment or other consumer contexts, but the FTC rule specifically targets AI-powered systems like emotion recognition and gait analysis, while the Oman rule is broader and less AI-specific.

Both impose a necessity/subsidiarity requirement on biometric systems, but China's rule specifically mandates avoiding facial recognition when non-biometric means can achieve the same purpose, while Oman's rule focuses on authorization before deployment.

Both rules address biometric identification systems requiring heightened oversight, but Peru's rule frames this as a high-risk AI classification trigger (real-time or post-hoc biometric identification, categorization, or analysis) while Oman's rule requires specific authorization before deployment in public or employment contexts — different legal mechanism and scope.

Both rules impose prior authorization requirements before deploying biometric identification systems in public contexts, but the Brazilian rule specifically targets real-time remote identification for law enforcement and requires judicial authorization, while the Omani rule requires administrative authorization and covers employment contexts as well.

rule_text: You must register your processing activities with the ITA in accordance with the procedures set out in the 2023 implementing regulations.
rule_text_technical: ITA implementing regulations issued in 2023 provide detailed procedures for registration of processing activities with the ITA.

first_instance.citation: Implementing Regulations 2023 — Registration of Processing Activities

instances.citation: Implementing Regulations 2023 — Registration of Processing Activities
instances.notes: Rule introduced in Oman PDPL 2022 (Oman, 2022-02-09).

instances.citation: UU PDP Art. (Cross-Border Transfer – Reporting and Continued Protection)
instances.notes: Both require reporting/registering data transfers with a supervisory authority, but the Indonesian UU PDP focuses specifically on cross-border transfers with an ongoing adequacy/protection obligation, whereas the Oman rule concerns general registration of processing activities with the ITA.

instances.citation: NDPA 2023, Registration of Data Controllers of Major Importance
instances.notes: Both require registration of (certain) data controllers with the supervisory authority, but the NDPA 2023 limits the obligation to 'data controllers of major importance' and adds an annual fee requirement, whereas the Oman rule applies more broadly to processing activities generally.

Both independently require controllers to register their processing activities with the national data protection authority, though Pakistan specifies a 'national register of controllers' and Oman references ITA procedures under implementing regulations.

Both require registration with a data protection authority before operating, but India's rule applies specifically to Consent Managers registering with the Data Protection Board, whereas Oman's rule covers general processing activities registered with the ITA.

Both require pre-market/pre-service registration with a designated government body, but this rule is specific to high-risk AI systems with the SNGD rather than general data processing activities with the ITA.

Both require registration of processing activities with a data protection authority, but the California rule is specific to data brokers, sets an annual January 31 deadline tied to qualifying thresholds, and is directed at a state-level agency rather than a general regulatory body.

Both require pre-commencement registration/notification with a competent authority, but the DGA rule targets data intermediation service providers specifically, while the Oman rule concerns personal data processing activities generally.

rule_text: You must comply with this Act even if another written law governs you, unless that other law provides personal data protection consistent with this Act.
rule_text_technical: The provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other written law relating to the protection of personal data of data subjects; however, public authorities governed by another written law may carry out processing in accordance with that law in so far as the protection of personal data is consistent with this Act.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Act, No. 9 of 2022 (Sri Lanka)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Sri Lanka Personal Data Protection Act 2022 (Sri Lanka, 2022-03-19).

Both address the relationship between the new law and existing legal frameworks, but the EU AI Act explicitly preserves existing Union law across multiple domains (data protection, consumer protection, fundamental rights), whereas Sri Lanka's PDPA establishes a general supremacy clause in conflicts with other written laws.

Both establish a general/lex generalis relationship with other sector-specific laws, but the Korean provision also requires future laws to align with this Act, whereas the Sri Lankan provision focuses on conflict resolution in favour of its own Act.

instances.citation: AI Promotion Act (General Framework) — Existing Legal Frameworks Preserved
instances.notes: Both rules address preservation of existing legal frameworks alongside the new AI-specific law, but Japan's rule broadly preserves sectoral laws, civil liability, criminal statutes, and APPI, while Sri Lanka's rule concerns precedence between the PDPA and other written laws on data protection.

rule_text: In any conflict between this Act and another written law concerning personal data protection, this Act prevails.
rule_text_technical: In the event of any inconsistency between the provisions of this Act and the provisions of such other written law, the provisions of this Act shall prevail.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Act, No. 9 of 2022 (Sri Lanka)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Sri Lanka Personal Data Protection Act 2022 (Sri Lanka, 2022-03-19).

rule_text: You may further process personal data for archiving, scientific, historical, or statistical purposes in the public interest without this being considered incompatible with the original purpose, subject to section 10.
rule_text_technical: Subject to section 10, further processing of personal data by a controller for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific research, historical research or statistical purposes shall not be considered to be incompatible with the initial purposes referred to in § 6(1).

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection Act, No. 9 of 2022 (Sri Lanka)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Sri Lanka Personal Data Protection Act 2022 (Sri Lanka, 2022-03-19).

Both permit processing of personal data for research, archiving, or statistical purposes as an exemption from standard obligations, with India adding a condition that the purpose is served without an action against the data principal.

rule_text: These Regulations apply to you if you conduct AI research, product design, development, manufacturing, sale, deployment, operation, or related support services within Shanghai's administrative area.
rule_text_technical: These Regulations apply to all entities and individuals within the administrative area of Shanghai engaged in: (1) AI technology research and development; (2) AI product design, development, manufacturing, and sale; (3) development, deployment, and operation of AI applications and services; (4) AI industry-related talent cultivation, investment, financing, and support services.

first_instance.law_name: Shanghai Municipality Regulations on the Promotion and Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Shanghai AI Industry Development Ordinance (Shanghai, 2022-09-25).

rule_text: You must employ technical measures to attach non-intrusive symbols to all information content produced or edited by users of your services, and store log information in accordance with laws, administrative regulations, and relevant state provisions.
rule_text_technical: Deep synthesis service providers shall employ technical measures to attach symbols to information content produced or edited by their services' users that do not impact users' usage, and store log information in accordance with laws, administrative regulations, and relevant state provisions.
