instances.citation: Measures Table – Transparency, Row 2 (Publicly Available Systems, Developers)
instances.notes: Both rules require a technical mechanism to identify AI-generated/synthesized content, but the Chinese binding rule mandates non-intrusive symbols and storage logs, while this voluntary Canadian recommendation focuses on freely available detection methods for the public, differing in obligation level, mechanism, and audience.

Both require labeling/identification of AI-generated synthetic content, but the Beijing rule explicitly cross-references the Deep Synthesis Provisions and covers text, pictures, audio, and video as a generative AI service obligation, whereas the Deep Synthesis rule focuses on non-intrusive symbols attached by service providers and storage requirements.

Both rules address attaching provenance/authentication markers (watermarks/symbols) to AI-generated content, but the G7 voluntary instrument is a soft-law recommendation with a 'where technically feasible' qualifier, while the Chinese rule is a binding mandate requiring non-intrusive symbols on all user-produced deep synthesis content.

instances.citation: Risk Category: Information Integrity / Synthetic Media
instances.notes: Both rules address technical and governance measures for detecting and managing AI-generated synthetic media, but the NIST rule is a voluntary recommendation for organizational implementation broadly, whereas the Chinese rule is a binding mandate requiring specific non-intrusive labeling and storage of synthetic content.

Both rules require embedding a non-visible/latent technical marker into AI-generated content, but California's rule applies broadly to all GenAI image/video/audio output and is framed as a mandatory latent disclosure, while China's rule ties the requirement to user-produced content and focuses on storage and traceability alongside the technical symbol.

Both require that labels be applied before content is displayed to users and prohibit distribution of unlabelled AI-generated content, though Art.17 frames this as a pre-display obligation while Art.16 of Deep Synthesis focuses on technical attachment and storage.

Both rules require technical measures (watermarking/metadata or non-intrusive symbols) to mark AI-generated or synthesized content, but the California AB 853 rule applies to image, video, and audio outputs with both manifest and latent disclosure mechanisms, while China's deep synthesis rule focuses on user-generated content storage and non-intrusive symbols without the manifest/latent dual-layer distinction.

Both impose obligations on operators to technically detect and label AI-generated content, but this rule is specific to network operators under the Cybersecurity Law targeting illegal information, while the existing rule applies to deep synthesis service providers and requires non-intrusive symbols on user-produced content.

Both require technical marking/labeling of AI-generated content, but Vietnam's rule mandates machine-readable format per government standards for providers, while China's rule requires non-intrusive symbols attached by service operators with storage obligations, reflecting different scope and technical specifics.

instances.citation: Mandatory Labeling Obligations for SSMIs — AI Content Labeling Requirement, ¶1
instances.notes: Both require technical measures to identify and label AI-generated content, but the Indian rule focuses on detection and labeling of user-uploaded content where the platform has knowledge, while the Chinese rule mandates attaching non-intrusive symbols and storing records for all user-produced content.

Both rules require embedding technical markers/metadata in AI-generated or synthetically modified content, but the Chinese rule specifies non-intrusive symbols with storage obligations and applies to user-produced content on platforms, while the Indian advisory mandates permanent unique metadata/identifiers embedded by the service provider itself, with broader coverage across text, audio, visual, and audio-visual modalities.

rule_text: Where you provide deep synthesis services that might cause confusion or mislead the public — including smart dialogue, voice synthesis, face generation/swapping, immersive scene generation, or other services that significantly alter information content — you must make a conspicuous label in a reasonable position alerting the public that the content is deep synthesis-generated.
rule_text_technical: Where deep synthesis service providers provide deep synthesis services which might cause confusion or mislead the public, including: (1) services simulating natural persons to generate or edit texts; (2) speech generation or editing services significantly changing personal identification characteristics; (3) services generating images or video of virtual persons or editing services significantly changing personal identification characteristics; (4) generation or editing services for realistic immersive scenes; (5) other services generating or significantly altering information content; they shall make a conspicuous label in a reasonable position or location on information content they generate or edit, alerting the public of the deep synthesis generation.

Both rules address AI-generated content that may mislead users or undermine authenticity, but this rule imposes an ethics review procedural requirement rather than a labeling/disclosure obligation, and operates at the pre-deployment governance level rather than at the point of service delivery.

Both rules require labeling of AI-generated content (images, video) under the Deep Synthesis Provisions, but this rule is a cross-reference obligation in a generative AI regulation with broader scope, while the existing rule specifies particular service types and a 'prominent labeling' standard for content likely to cause public confusion.

Both require disclosure/labeling of AI-generated synthetic content, but the Michigan rule is narrowly scoped to political advertisements while the Chinese rule covers a broader range of deep synthesis services and focuses on public confusion rather than electoral context.

Both require disclosure/labeling when AI-generated content could confuse or mislead users about its synthetic nature, but the Chinese rule focuses on deep synthesis services with specific enumerated techniques, while the FTC rule targets impersonation of human representatives in consumer-facing interactions.

Both rules address disclosure/labeling of AI-generated or synthetic media content, but the Japanese guideline is a voluntary recommendation encouraging disclosure for user awareness, whereas the Chinese rule is a binding mandate requiring prominent labeling for specific deep synthesis services that may confuse the public.

Both rules require prominent/manifest disclosure on AI-generated or synthesized content, but California's rule frames it as a user-facing opt-in manifest disclosure offered by the provider, while China's rule imposes a mandatory prominent labeling obligation on the provider for content likely to cause public confusion, reflecting different obligation structures and scope.

Both require labelling of AI-generated/synthesized content with primary responsibility on the provider, but GB45438-2025 Art.4 establishes a general primary-responsibility framework while the Deep Synthesis rule specifies particular content types triggering prominent labelling.

Both rules require disclosure/labeling when AI-generated content could confuse or mislead users, but the Connecticut provision is a voluntary recommendation covering text broadly, while the Chinese binding rule mandates prominent labeling for specific deep synthesis services (dialogue, voice, face generation, etc.).

Both address content moderation obligations covering deepfakes and synthetic media, but this rule targets network operators under a cybersecurity framework and explicitly includes AI-generated disinformation, whereas the existing rule targets deep synthesis service providers with a prominent-labeling mandate for confusion-causing content.

Both rules require labeling of deep synthesis/synthetic content including deepfakes, but the Kazakhstan rule specifically mandates machine-readable labeling and a visible indicator for users, whereas the Chinese rule focuses on prominent disclosure to prevent public confusion across enumerated service types without specifying machine-readable format.

Both require deployers/service providers to prominently notify or label the public when AI-generated or AI-modified content could cause confusion, but Vietnam's rule covers text, audio, image and video broadly while China's rule is tied to specific deep synthesis service types and a confusion/mislead standard.

Both require conspicuous disclosure/labeling of AI-generated synthetic content, but the New York rule is narrowly scoped to advertising featuring synthetic performers, whereas the Chinese rule applies broadly to deep synthesis services that may cause public confusion across multiple content types.

instances.citation: Mandatory Labeling Obligations for SSMIs — AI Content Labeling Requirement, ¶2
instances.notes: Both require mandatory labeling of AI-generated content at point of creation, but the Indian rule specifically addresses platform-built AI tools applying labels at creation time, while the Chinese rule focuses on prominent labeling for content that could confuse or mislead the public across a range of deep synthesis service types.

instances.citation: Law No. 5651 Amendment — Deepfake Labelling (§ Labelling Obligation)
instances.notes: Both require prominent labeling of deepfake/deep synthesis content depicting real persons, but Turkey mandates a specific Turkish-language disclosure phrase ('yapay zeka ile üretilmiştir') while China's rule focuses on confusion/misleading potential and covers a broader set of synthesis types without specifying label language.

rule_text: For deep synthesis services not covered by the prominent-labeling mandate, you must still provide users with a prominent-labeling function and alert users that they may apply such labels.
rule_text_technical: Where deep synthesis service providers provide deep synthesis services other than those provided for in the preceding paragraph, they shall provide functions for prominently labeling, and alert deep synthesis service users that they may make prominent labels.

rule_text: You cannot use technical measures or any other means to delete, alter, or conceal the deep synthesis labels required under Articles 16 and 17.
rule_text_technical: Technical measures must not be employed by any organization or individual to delete, alter, or conceal the deep synthesis labels provided for in Articles 16 and 17 of these Provisions.

Both prohibit undermining AI-content labeling requirements, but the Deep Synthesis rule targets deletion, alteration, or concealment of labels by providers, while the Beijing rule focuses on providers helping users evade identification, shifting the framing to user-assistance rather than direct provider manipulation.

Both prohibit removal or concealment of AI-generated content labels and require technical safeguards to enforce this, though Art.16 places the obligation on platforms to prevent user-side removal while the Deep Synthesis rule is broader in scope.

instances.citation: Mandatory Labeling Obligations for SSMIs — Synthetic Media Enhanced Labeling, ¶2(c)
instances.notes: Both address the persistence and tamper-resistance of synthetic media labels, but the Chinese rule prohibits deletion or concealment of labels by providers, while the Indian rule affirmatively requires labels to be resistant to cropping/editing and to persist through download or screen-capture.

rule_text: After completing filing, you must display your filing number and provide a link to publicly displayed filing information on your websites and applications.
rule_text_technical: Deep synthesis service providers and technical supporters that have completed filings shall indicate their filing number and provide links to publicly displayed information on the websites, applications, and so forth that they provide.

rule_text: Organizations should understand, manage, and document legal and regulatory requirements involving AI systems applicable to their context.
rule_text_technical: Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are to be understood, managed, and documented as part of organizational AI risk governance processes.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (NIST, 2023-01-26).

Both require organizations to integrate AI risk management into governance structures, but ISO 23894 is a voluntary standard emphasizing integration into broader governance, while NIST AI RMF focuses on understanding and documenting legal and regulatory requirements.

Both rules require compliance with applicable legal and regulatory requirements governing the relevant activities, but this rule is a binding Chinese regulation covering scientific and technological activities broadly including ethics standards, whereas the NIST rule is a voluntary framework recommendation focused on AI risk management.

Both address reviewing and updating existing legislation to address AI governance needs, but Tunisia's rule is a voluntary recommendation to update data protection, cybersecurity, and digital economy laws while the NIST framework recommends organizations understand and document legal requirements; both are non-binding but differ in actor and scope.

instances.notes: Both require organizations to implement risk management frameworks for AI, but the Canada voluntary code is a soft-law instrument recommending proportionate risk management proportionate to activity profile, while the NIST AI RMF focuses on understanding and documenting legal/regulatory requirements; scope and obligation level differ.

Both call for organizations to understand and manage AI risks through governance policies, but the G7 rule is voluntary and broader in scope (adding privacy, risk disclosure, and risk-based approach framing), while NIST AI RMF is also voluntary but more narrowly focused on documenting legal/regulatory requirements.

Both address the requirement to understand and comply with legal and regulatory requirements for AI systems, but the Spain sandbox rule is specific to EU/national regulations including RRF, while the NIST rule is a broader voluntary framework recommendation.

Both address planning for AI-related risks and opportunities within an organizational governance framework, but ISO 42001 frames this as a formal AIMS planning clause requiring documented actions, while NIST GOVERN-1-1 focuses on understanding and documenting legal and regulatory requirements.

Both rules concern applying NIST AI RMF governance structures to AI risk management, but this rule specifically addresses mapping mitigations to all four AI RMF functions in the context of generative AI, which is more specific than the existing rule's general legal/regulatory compliance documentation requirement.

Both require organizations to understand and comply with legal and regulatory requirements for AI systems, but this EO rule is a voluntary federal agency recommendation focused on constitutional and statutory consistency, while the NIST rule is a broader voluntary framework for documenting legal requirements.

Both address organizational AI risk management policies and accountability structures, but the DHS rule focuses specifically on critical infrastructure context and is voluntary guidance, while the NIST AI RMF rule addresses understanding and documenting legal/regulatory requirements more broadly.

Both require compliance with applicable law and coordination of AI-related legal obligations, but this rule is a binding agency directive requiring cross-agency coordination of compliance with OMB policies, while the NIST rule is a voluntary framework recommendation to understand and document legal requirements.

rule_text: Organizations should maintain an inventory of AI systems, resourced according to risk priorities.
rule_text_technical: Mechanisms are to be in place to inventory AI systems, resourced according to risk priorities.

first_instance.law_name: NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (NIST, 2023-01-26).

Both recommend maintaining an inventory/registry of AI systems, but this rule is scoped to the national public administration and assigned to a specific secretariat, whereas the NIST AI RMF rule applies to organizations generally with risk-prioritized resourcing; both are voluntary/recommendatory instruments.

Both rules involve institutional accountability for AI systems, but the Kentucky rule imposes a binding legislative reporting obligation (annual transmission of AI-use reports to oversight bodies) whereas the NIST AI RMF rule is a voluntary recommendation to maintain an AI inventory prioritized by risk, making the coverage, obligation level, and mechanism meaningfully different.

Both recommend maintaining an inventory of AI systems, but this rule adds the specific element of identifying regulatory barriers to AI adoption and is scoped to federal agencies under an executive order, whereas the NIST AI RMF rule is a broader organizational recommendation prioritized by risk.

instances.citation: Implementation Requirements — Agency Consistency Plans (inventory and plan requirement)
instances.notes: Both rules concern maintaining an inventory of AI systems and documenting their use, but this rule is a time-bound agency-level planning and conformity-documentation requirement from a voluntary executive order, while the NIST AI RMF rule is a broader voluntary recommendation to maintain an AI inventory resourced by risk priority.

Both require maintaining an inventory of AI systems, but the new rule is a binding federal agency obligation that also mandates updating compliance plans and reporting, whereas the NIST AI RMF rule is a voluntary framework recommendation focused solely on maintaining an AI system inventory resourced by risk priority.

rule_text: Organizations should establish processes for safely decommissioning and phasing out AI systems.
rule_text_technical: Processes are to be in place for safely decommissioning and phasing out AI systems in a manner consistent with risk management objectives.

rule_text: Organizations should ensure executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment.
rule_text_technical: Executive leadership is to take responsibility for decisions about risks associated with AI system development and deployment.

Both require top/executive leadership to take responsibility for AI governance and set direction, but ISO 42001 is a voluntary management system standard focused on policy-objective alignment within an AIMS, while NIST AI RMF focuses on executive accountability for risk decisions; scope and framing differ.

Both rules address organizational accountability for AI outcomes and leadership responsibility, but the UN resolution is a soft-law recommendation covering developers, deployers, and users with 'clear responsibility chains,' while NIST AI RMF focuses specifically on executive leadership taking responsibility for risk decisions.

Both address internal organizational governance for AI, but this rule targets business users of AI (operators) establishing internal governance policies, whereas the NIST rule focuses on executive leadership accountability for AI risk decisions in developing/deploying organizations.

instances.citation: Bill Summary – Affirmative Defense: Compliance with Recognized Risk Management Framework
instances.notes: Both rules relate to AI risk management frameworks as a governance mechanism, but Colorado's rule creates a binding affirmative legal defense tied to compliance with recognized frameworks, whereas the NIST rule is a voluntary recommendation about executive accountability for AI risk decisions.

Both require organizational governance structures for AI risk management and assign responsibility to leadership, but NIST AI 600-1 specifically extends GOVERN function guidance to GenAI-specific risks, whereas the existing NIST AI RMF rule focuses on executive accountability for AI risk decisions more broadly.

Both require that executive/senior leadership take responsibility for AI risk decisions, but NIST AI RMF is also a voluntary framework with slightly different framing around risk responsibility vs. being 'informed of material AI risks'; the concepts are substantively the same but phrased and scoped differently.

Both rules require organizational-level governance structures with executive or legislative accountability for responsible and ethical AI use, but the Kentucky rule establishes a specific statutory committee with formal mandate under state law, whereas the NIST AI RMF rule is a voluntary framework recommendation for executive leadership responsibility.

instances.citation: § OMB Coordination — Federal AI Governance Framework
instances.notes: Both address executive-level responsibility for AI governance frameworks within government/organizations, but this new rule specifically recommends OMB issue an updated federal AI governance framework within 180 days for federal agencies, whereas the NIST AI RMF rule addresses organizational executive leadership taking responsibility for AI risk decisions more broadly.

Both rules address accountability for AI governance, but Taiwan's Art. 4(7) frames this as a principle requiring responsibility to accompany AI promotion (internal and external governance), while NIST AI RMF Govern 2.3 focuses specifically on executive leadership taking responsibility for risk decisions in development and deployment contexts; Taiwan's rule is broader in scope and comes from a binding statute rather than a voluntary framework.

instances.citation: Principle 1 — Internal Governance Structures and Measures (Board and Senior Leadership Accountability)
instances.notes: Both require executive/senior leadership accountability for AI risk decisions, but the NIST rule is a voluntary framework recommendation focusing on risk decisions while the SG rule is also voluntary but frames it as awareness of AI strategy and risk posture broadly.

Both require that accountable officials or executive leadership take responsibility for AI systems and their associated risks, but this EO rule specifically requires identifying a named accountable official per AI application in federal agencies, while the NIST rule more broadly addresses executive responsibility for AI risk decisions.

Both require organizational accountability for AI outcomes at a senior/executive level, but the UK White Paper frames this as a voluntary principle for organizations commensurate with risk, while NIST RMF specifically calls for executive leadership responsibility over AI risk decisions.

Both address designating accountable individuals for AI risk management decisions, but the DHS rule is voluntary guidance for critical infrastructure contexts while the NIST rule focuses on executive leadership responsibility.

instances.notes: Both are voluntary instruments recommending coordinated safety evaluation and information sharing, but the Seoul commitment is specifically directed at frontier AI companies participating in an international AI Safety Institute network, whereas the NIST rule addresses organizational-level testing and incident information sharing practices.

Both require taking measures to improve AI/model output accuracy and quality on an ongoing basis, but the FTC rule is specifically tied to consumer assessments under consumer protection law (likely FCRA context), while the Beijing rule focuses broadly on training data quality and diversity.

Both require improving training data quality including accuracy, relevance, and representativeness, but ISO 42001 is a voluntary management standard while the Beijing GenAI rule is a binding regulation with mandatory obligations.

Both require improving training data quality including accuracy and representativeness to avoid biased or discriminatory outputs, but this is a voluntary Hong Kong guidance recommendation while the existing rule is a binding Chinese municipal regulation with a broader mandate covering truthfulness, objectivity, and diversity.

Both rules require improving training data quality including accuracy and reducing bias/improving diversity, but the Beijing rule is a binding mandate while this is a voluntary recommendation, and the Beijing rule emphasizes authenticity, objectivity, and diversity more explicitly.

Both rules address data cleaning, processing, and modification of training datasets, but the California rule requires public disclosure of whether such modifications occurred and their intended purpose, whereas the Beijing rule imposes an internal obligation to take effective measures to improve data quality and truthfulness.

Both require improving training data quality and representativeness, but Ontario Bill 194 frames this as a binding risk management obligation for public sector AI systems rather than a generative AI-specific requirement, and uses the concept of 'accuracy and representativeness' rather than the Chinese rule's emphasis on 'authenticity, accuracy, objectivity, and diversity'.

Both independently require data governance practices over training, validation, and testing datasets covering quality dimensions, though the Peru rule is framed as a high-risk AI obligation and the Beijing rule is phrased as a general improvement mandate with slightly different scope.

Both rules require ensuring quality, accuracy, and reliability of AI training data, but the Italian rule adds security, appropriateness, and transparency dimensions and applies broadly to AI development processes rather than specifically to generative AI training data.

Both require improving training data quality along dimensions relevant to bias and representativeness, but the Brazilian rule specifically mandates representative datasets to minimize bias against legally protected characteristics, while the Beijing rule focuses more broadly on authenticity, accuracy, objectivity, and diversity without tying the requirement to anti-discrimination law.

Both prohibit use of illegal data for training and address harmful content, but this rule from a voluntary framework also covers false, biased, and IP-infringing content, while the Beijing rule is a binding mandate narrowly focused on unlawfully obtained internet-scraped data.

Both rules impose criminal penalties for knowingly violating AI political content disclosure/prohibition requirements, but Indiana imposes a Level 6 felony (a more serious criminal classification) while Michigan imposes only a misdemeanor with a fine cap, and Indiana's mens rea includes 'recklessly' in addition to 'intentionally' and 'knowingly'.

Both impose criminal penalties (misdemeanor) for AI-disclosure violations in elections, but Alabama's penalty is substantially higher (up to 1 year jail and $6,000 fine vs. Michigan's lower misdemeanor fine) and applies to a broader deceptive-media prohibition rather than just disclaimer requirements.

Both rules impose criminal penalties (misdemeanor) for violating AI/synthetic media disclosure requirements in political advertising, but Arizona SB 1359 adds an escalating penalty structure (enhanced consequences within five years of a prior conviction) while Michigan PA 263/266 sets a flat fine cap of up to a specific dollar amount without the recidivism escalation.

Both impose criminal penalties (fine and/or imprisonment) for violations of an AI-related statute, but Louisiana's rule targets nonconsensual AI-generated intimate images with up to 6 months imprisonment and $750 fine, while the Michigan rule targets AI disclosure violations as a misdemeanor with a different fine structure and context.

Both rules impose misdemeanor criminal liability for knowing violations of AI-related election disclosure/prohibition requirements, but Michigan's rule specifies a fine up to a particular amount for identification/disclaimer violations while Nevada's targets creation or distribution of materially deceptive AI-generated media.

Both impose criminal misdemeanor penalties for knowing violations related to AI-generated content in election contexts, but Hawaii targets distributing materially deceptive AI-generated media in elections while Michigan targets violations of AI disclosure/disclaimer requirements for political advertisements.

Both rules impose criminal misdemeanor penalties for knowing violations of AI-related election disclosure requirements, but differ in jurisdiction, specific penalty amounts, and the NC rule adds escalation to a Class I felony for subsequent violations within a specified period.

Both impose criminal penalties (fines and/or imprisonment) for violations of AI disclosure/identification requirements in political advertising, but differ in jurisdiction, penalty amounts (SGD 1,000 vs USD 500), availability of imprisonment, and the specific electoral advertising context covered.

Both impose criminal penalties for violating AI-related political content disclosure/labeling requirements, but Michigan's rule specifies a misdemeanor with a fine up to an unstated amount while South Dakota's rule specifies a Class 1 misdemeanor carrying up to one year imprisonment, differing in penalty structure and offense classification.

Both laws criminalize failure to include required AI-content disclaimers in political communications, but Michigan's rule specifies a misdemeanor with a fine up to a stated amount while North Dakota's rule truncates before specifying the penalty tier, and the jurisdictional scope and exact disclaimer requirements differ.

Both criminalize knowing violations of AI political communication disclosure/prohibition requirements as misdemeanors, but Rhode Island's law sets a fine range of $500–$5,000 with escalation to a felony on subsequent offenses, while Michigan's caps at a different fine amount with no escalating felony tier specified in that provision.

rule_text_technical: This section does not apply to a qualified political advertisement that constitutes satire or parody.

first_instance.law_name: Michigan Public Acts 263-266 — AI in Political Advertising Package

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Michigan PA 263-266 (Deepfakes in Elections) (Michigan, 2023-11-15).

Both rules exempt satirical or parodic AI-generated political content, but New Mexico adds a contextual clarity condition ('presented in a context that makes the satirical nature clear') not present in Michigan's briefer exemption.
Both Indiana and Michigan independently exempt satire or parody from their respective AI political content requirements, though Indiana adds the condition that the content be identified as such.

Both exempt satire or parody from the law's requirements, but Georgia adds a 'clearly labeled' and 'reasonable person' standard whereas Michigan's exemption applies only to qualified political advertisements without labeling requirements.

Both exempt satire and parody from AI-related political content obligations, though Alabama's rule specifies the content must be 'clearly presented' as satirical or comedic while Michigan's exemption lacks that qualifier.

Both rules exempt parody and satire from the synthetic/digitally altered media prohibition, and Arizona additionally exempts commentary, criticism, and artistic expression; the underlying concept is the same but Arizona's exemption is broader in scope.
Both exempt synthetic media or AI-generated content that constitutes satire or parody from the political advertising disclosure requirements, using nearly identical substantive language.
Both exempt obvious satire or parody that a reasonable person would identify as such, though Nevada's rule applies to the broader prohibition rather than just disclosure requirements.

Both exempt satire and parody from synthetic media restrictions, but California's rule also adds comment, criticism, and scholarship as exempt purposes and applies to deceased personality digital replicas rather than AI-generated political advertisements.

Both exempt satirical or parody content from AI disclosure or prohibition requirements, but Singapore's rule adds a 'clearly labelled' condition and a 'no reasonable person would believe' standard, while Michigan's rule simply exempts satire or parody without those additional conditions.

Both provide defenses to liability related to synthetic media in political communications, but Kentucky frames this as an affirmative defense based on conspicuous disclosure rather than a categorical exemption for satire/parody.

Both exempt satire and parody from AI/deepfake political content disclosure or labeling requirements, with SD SB164 adding a reasonable-person standard to assess whether content would be understood as satirical.

rule_text: A business or its affiliate regulated by the Michigan Public Service Commission or the Federal Communications Commission is exempt from the AI disclosure requirements of this section.
rule_text_technical: This section does not apply to a business or its affiliate if the business or its affiliate is regulated by the Michigan public service commission or the Federal Communications Commission.

first_instance.law_name: Michigan Public Acts 263-266 — AI in Political Advertising Package

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Michigan PA 263-266 (Deepfakes in Elections) (Michigan, 2023-11-15).

rule_text: A distribution platform is not liable for the absence of AI disclosure in a qualified political advertisement or prerecorded telephone message if the platform can demonstrate that it provided notice of its prohibition on the lack of such disclosure to the advertiser.
rule_text_technical: A distribution platform, as described in subsection (4)(c), is not liable for the lack of disclosure content created in whole or substantially by artificial intelligence in a qualified political advertisement or prerecorded telephone message if the distribution platform can show that the distribution platform provided notice of its prohibitions related to a lack of disclosure of content created in whole or substantially by artificial intelligence in a qualified political advertisement or prerecorded telephone message.

first_instance.law_name: Michigan Public Acts 263-266 — AI in Political Advertising Package

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Michigan PA 263-266 (Deepfakes in Elections) (Michigan, 2023-11-15).

Both rules exempt distribution platforms (broadcasters/carriers) from liability for AI disclosure violations in political communications, but Michigan's rule specifically addresses absence of disclosure while Wisconsin's rule addresses disclosure violations more broadly, and the drafting and scope differ.

Both rules provide liability protection for online platforms regarding AI-generated political content, but Michigan's rule is a specific non-liability carve-out for absence of disclosure, while NC's rule is an affirmative safe harbor contingent on establishing and enforcing takedown policies.

rule_text: You must have competent and reliable evidence to support any claims about the performance, accuracy, or capabilities of your AI systems before making such claims to consumers.
rule_text_technical: Businesses must possess competent and reliable evidence to substantiate material representations about the performance, accuracy, or capabilities of AI systems, including claims of accuracy, lack of bias, or superiority to human performance, prior to making such claims in commerce.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Decision-Making

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC AI Policy Statement (2023) (FTC, 2023-11-21).

Both address preventing misrepresentation of AI capabilities and limitations, but the FTC rule is a binding requirement to have competent evidence before making claims, while this is a voluntary recommendation against deceptive practices more broadly covering nature, capabilities, and limitations.

rule_text: You cannot use AI to generate fake consumer reviews, fabricate celebrity endorsements, or create false impressions of widespread consumer satisfaction.
rule_text_technical: Under the FTC's Endorsement Guides (16 C.F.R. Part 255) and Section 5 of the FTC Act, businesses may not use AI to generate fake consumer reviews, fabricate celebrity endorsements, or manufacture the appearance of consumer or expert approval, as such conduct constitutes a deceptive practice.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Decision-Making

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC AI Policy Statement (2023) (FTC, 2023-11-21).

rule_text: You cannot avoid FTC Act liability for discriminatory AI outcomes by attributing those outcomes to the AI system itself.
rule_text_technical: Businesses cannot avoid liability under the FTC Act by attributing discriminatory outcomes to an AI system that they deploy; deployers of AI systems remain responsible for discriminatory outcomes produced by those systems.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Decision-Making

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC AI Policy Statement (2023) (FTC, 2023-11-21).

instances.citation: AB 316 § (Prohibition on the Autonomous AI Defense)
instances.notes: Both rules reject the use of AI autonomy as a shield against liability, but the FTC rule targets discriminatory outcomes under the FTC Act while AB 316 broadly prohibits asserting AI autonomous causation as a complete civil defense regardless of harm type.

Both establish that AI developers/providers cannot escape liability by attributing harmful outcomes to the AI system itself, but this rule specifically addresses joint liability for cyberattacks based on knowing the system's attack capabilities, whereas the existing rule concerns FTC Act liability for discriminatory AI outcomes.

instances.citation: Law No. 6563 & Law No. 6698 Amendment — Joint Liability (§ Developer Liability)
instances.notes: Both rules address developer/provider liability for harmful AI-generated content, but the Turkey rule establishes joint civil liability for developers who knew or should have known of harmful outputs, while the FTC rule focuses on prohibiting companies from deflecting regulatory liability onto the AI system itself.

Both establish that liability for discriminatory AI outcomes is impact-based and cannot be avoided by attributing outcomes to the AI system itself, though Brazil's rule frames this as a general statutory obligation while the FTC rule is an enforcement policy interpretation.

rule_text: You cannot use AI to personalize or optimize manipulative interface designs that exploit consumer psychology to override autonomous consumer decision-making.
rule_text_technical: Using AI to personalize and optimize manipulative interface designs—including dark patterns—that exploit consumer psychology to override autonomous decision-making constitutes an unfair practice and an enforcement priority under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Decision-Making

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC AI Policy Statement (2023) (FTC, 2023-11-21).

Both prohibit deceptive AI-driven interactions that undermine consumer autonomy, but the FTC rule targets manipulative interface design exploiting consumer psychology broadly, while this Florida rule specifically prohibits chatbots designed to deceive consumers into thinking they are communicating with a human.

Both prohibit AI-driven manipulation of user behavior/psychology, but the Kazakhstan rule is broader (general 'manipulative techniques' on subconscious/behavior) while the FTC rule targets specifically personalized/optimized manipulative interface designs exploiting consumer psychology.

Both prohibit using AI to exploit psychological vulnerabilities of users, but Vietnam's rule explicitly targets vulnerable groups (children, elderly, disabled) with a broader prohibition on exploitation, while the FTC rule focuses on manipulative interface designs overriding consumer autonomy.

Both address prohibiting manipulative AI engagement techniques that override autonomous decision-making, but this rule is narrower (AI companion chatbots, minors only) while the FTC rule is broader (any AI, any consumer psychology manipulation).

Both prohibit AI exploitation of human psychological vulnerabilities to override autonomous decision-making, but the Russian provision is broader, explicitly enumerating age-related, cognitive, socio-economic, and physical characteristics, while the FTC rule focuses narrowly on manipulative interface designs targeting consumer psychology.

Both prohibit manipulative interface designs that undermine user autonomy, but DSA Art. 25 applies broadly to all online interfaces on digital service providers and is a binding EU regulation, whereas the FTC policy targets AI-specific personalization/optimization and is a softer instrument with narrower AI focus.

Both prohibit AI-driven manipulation exploiting consumer psychology, but Art. 5(1)(a) is a binding EU prohibition covering subliminal and purposefully manipulative techniques broadly, while the FTC rule is a US policy instrument focused on manipulative interface designs overriding autonomous consumer decisions.

Both prohibit AI-enabled manipulative techniques exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, but the Brazilian rule is a binding statutory prohibition covering development, offer, or use of such AI systems broadly, while the FTC rule is a policy-level instrument focused specifically on manipulative interface designs overriding consumer decision-making.

rule_text: You cannot use AI to infer sensitive personal information from non-sensitive data and then use those inferences to target or harm consumers.
rule_text_technical: Using AI to infer sensitive personal information from non-sensitive data and employing those inferences to target or harm consumers constitutes a potentially unfair practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Decision-Making

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC AI Policy Statement (2023) (FTC, 2023-11-21).

Both prohibit using biometric/AI technology for targeted commercial purposes exploiting individuals, but the FTC rule focuses on inferring sensitive data for harm while this rule specifically bans facial recognition for inducing purchases and analyzing consumer behavior in physical premises.

rule_text: If your company sells AI-generated risk scores or consumer assessments related to creditworthiness, insurance eligibility, employment, or housing, you may be operating as a consumer reporting agency subject to full FCRA obligations.
rule_text_technical: Companies that sell AI-powered scores or assessments bearing on consumer creditworthiness, insurance eligibility, employment, or housing may be operating as consumer reporting agencies (CRAs) subject to the full obligations of the Fair Credit Reporting Act, including obligations related to accuracy, disputes, and permissible purpose, where such assessments constitute 'consumer reports' as defined under the FCRA.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Decision-Making

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC AI Policy Statement (2023) (FTC, 2023-11-21).

rule_text: You must provide consumers with written adverse action notices when denying credit, insurance, employment, or housing based in whole or in part on an AI-generated assessment that constitutes a consumer report.
rule_text_technical: Users of AI systems that constitute consumer reports must comply with FCRA adverse action notification requirements; when an adverse action is taken based in whole or in part on an AI-generated assessment, the user must provide the consumer with a written notice of the adverse action, identify the consumer reporting agency that provided the report, and include a statement of the consumer's right to obtain a free copy of the report and to dispute inaccurate information.

first_instance.law_name: FTC Policy Statement on Artificial Intelligence and Algorithmic Decision-Making

instances.notes: Rule introduced in FTC AI Policy Statement (2023) (FTC, 2023-11-21).

rule_text: You must design and manufacture connected products — and design and provide related services — so that product data is accessible to the user by default, easily, securely, and free of charge, in a comprehensive, structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format.
rule_text_technical: Connected products shall be designed and manufactured, and related services shall be designed and provided, such that product data is, by default, easily, securely, and free of charge accessible to the user in a comprehensive, structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format, and directly accessible where technically feasible.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Before concluding a purchase contract, you must disclose to users the type and format of data the connected product can generate, whether data is stored on-device or remotely, retention periods, and methods of access and erasure.
rule_text_technical: Prior to conclusion of a purchase contract for a connected product or related service, sellers must disclose: the type and format of data the product can generate, whether data is stored on-device or remotely, applicable retention periods, and the methods by which data may be accessed and erased.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

Both rules require pre-market or pre-contractual disclosure about product characteristics to enable informed user decisions, but the CRA targets cybersecurity support period transparency for digital products, while the Data Act targets data generation/storage capabilities of connected products.

rule_text: You cannot make data access unduly difficult through non-neutral means.
rule_text_technical: Data holders are prohibited from making access to data unduly difficult through the use of non-neutral means or practices that obstruct effective access.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot coerce, deceive, or manipulate users in relation to data access.
rule_text_technical: Data holders are prohibited from using coercion, deception, or manipulation of users in connection with data access or the exercise of data access rights.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot retain unnecessary access logs when making data available to users.
rule_text_technical: Data holders are prohibited from retaining access logs that are not necessary in the context of making data available to users.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Where trade secrets are involved, you must apply proportionate technical and organisational measures and require confidentiality agreements before disclosing data.
rule_text_technical: Where data sharing involves the disclosure of trade secrets, data holders must implement proportionate technical and organisational protection measures and may require the conclusion of confidentiality agreements prior to disclosure.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You may suspend data sharing if a user or third party fails to implement agreed confidentiality measures for trade secrets.
rule_text_technical: Data holders may suspend the making available of data where confidentiality measures required for the protection of trade secrets have not been implemented by the user or third party requesting access.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: In exceptional circumstances, you may refuse data access if you can demonstrate that sharing would likely cause serious economic damage.
rule_text_technical: In exceptional circumstances, data holders may refuse to make data available where they can demonstrate to the competent authority that doing so would likely result in serious economic damage to the data holder.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Gatekeepers designated under the Digital Markets Act cannot be eligible third parties for the purposes of receiving data under Article 5.
rule_text_technical: Undertakings designated as gatekeepers pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (Digital Markets Act) are excluded from eligibility as third parties for the purpose of receiving data under Article 5.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Third parties cannot use coercive means to access data or use data to derive competitive insights about the data holder.
rule_text_technical: Third parties are prohibited from using coercive means to obtain data access and from using data received under Article 5 to derive insights about the competitive position, assets, or activities of the data holder.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You must comply with EU data protection law when processing any personal data received under Chapter II.
rule_text_technical: Third parties receiving data under Chapter II must ensure that processing of any personal data included therein complies with applicable Union data protection law.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot profile users using data received under Chapter II, except where strictly necessary to provide the agreed service.
rule_text_technical: Third parties receiving data under Chapter II are prohibited from profiling users using such data, except where profiling is strictly necessary for the provision of the service requested by the user.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot share data received under Chapter II with other third parties unless contractually authorised to do so.
rule_text_technical: Third parties receiving data under Chapter II are prohibited from making such data available to other third parties unless expressly authorised by the terms of the contract concluded with the user.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot make data received under Chapter II available to gatekeepers.
rule_text_technical: Third parties receiving data under Chapter II are prohibited from making such data available to undertakings designated as gatekeepers under Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot use data received under Chapter II to develop a product that competes with the connected product from which the data was generated.
rule_text_technical: Third parties receiving data under Chapter II are prohibited from using such data for the purpose of developing a product or related service that competes with the connected product or related service from which the data originates.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot ignore agreed confidentiality measures for trade secrets contained in data received under Chapter II.
rule_text_technical: Third parties receiving data under Chapter II must comply with any confidentiality measures agreed for the protection of trade secrets contained in such data and may not circumvent or ignore such measures.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Chapter II obligations do not apply to data generated by microenterprises or small enterprises unless they are acting as subcontractors.
rule_text_technical: The obligations set out in Chapter II do not apply to data holders that qualify as microenterprises or small enterprises within the meaning of Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC, unless they are acting in the capacity of subcontractors.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Medium-sized enterprises that recently qualified as such are exempt from Chapter II obligations for one year following that qualification.
rule_text_technical: Medium-sized enterprises that have recently ceased to qualify as small enterprises, and thereby newly qualify as medium-sized enterprises, are exempt from the obligations of Chapter II for a transitional period of one year from the date of such qualification.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Where you are obliged under Union law to make data available, you must do so under fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) terms and conditions in a transparent manner.
rule_text_technical: Where a data holder is subject to an obligation under Union law to make data available to data recipients, such data must be made available under fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory terms and conditions and in a transparent manner.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You must treat comparable categories of data recipients uniformly when making data available under Union law obligations.
rule_text_technical: Data holders subject to Union law obligations to make data available must apply equivalent terms and conditions to data recipients belonging to comparable categories, ensuring non-discriminatory treatment.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Exclusive data access arrangements in B2B settings are only permitted where justified by a user request under Chapter II.
rule_text_technical: Exclusive data access arrangements between data holders and data recipients in business-to-business relations are permissible only where they arise from a specific user request made pursuant to Chapter II.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Compensation agreed between data holders and data recipients must be non-discriminatory and reasonable.
rule_text_technical: Any compensation agreed between data holders and data recipients for making data available under obligations imposed by Union law must be non-discriminatory and reasonable in amount.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: When calculating compensation, you must take into account the costs of formatting and disseminating data, as well as investments in data collection and production.
rule_text_technical: Compensation for making data available must be calculated with due regard to the costs of formatting and disseminating the data and to the investments made in the collection and production of the data.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Where the data recipient is an SME or not-for-profit research organisation, compensation is capped at direct costs and may not include a return on investment.
rule_text_technical: Where the data recipient is a small or medium-sized enterprise or a not-for-profit research organisation, the compensation recoverable by the data holder is capped at the direct costs of making the data available, excluding any return on investment.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: The Commission must develop guidelines on compensation calculation to assist data holders and data recipients.
rule_text_technical: The European Commission is required to develop and publish guidelines providing guidance on the calculation of reasonable compensation for making data available, to assist data holders and data recipients in complying with their obligations.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Dispute settlement bodies must be impartial and independent and possess the necessary expertise.
rule_text_technical: Certified dispute settlement bodies must operate in an impartial and independent manner and must possess the expertise necessary to effectively adjudicate disputes concerning data access and use obligations.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Dispute settlement bodies must adopt decisions within 90 days of receiving a request.
rule_text_technical: Certified dispute settlement bodies are required to adopt a decision within 90 calendar days of receipt of a complete request for dispute settlement.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You may apply technical protection measures such as smart contracts and encryption to prevent unauthorised data access, provided such measures do not discriminate between recipients or hinder user rights.
rule_text_technical: Data holders may implement technical protection measures, including smart contracts and encryption, to prevent unauthorised access to data, on condition that such measures do not discriminate between data recipients in comparable situations and do not hinder the exercise of rights conferred on users under this Regulation.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: Third parties and data recipients must comply with data holder requests to erase data, cease production of goods derived from unlawfully used data, and provide compensation for misuse.
rule_text_technical: Third parties and data recipients are obliged to comply with requests from data holders to erase data obtained without authorisation, to cease the production of goods or services derived from unlawfully used data, and to provide compensation for any damages resulting from such misuse.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: A contractual term concerning data access, use, liability, or remedies that is unilaterally imposed by one enterprise on another and is unfair is not binding on the party on whom it is imposed.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term concerning data access, data use, liability, or remedies that has been unilaterally imposed by one enterprise on another enterprise is not binding on the enterprise on whom it is imposed if it is unfair within the meaning of this Article.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: A contractual term is unfair if it grossly deviates from good commercial practice in data access and use, contrary to good faith and fair dealing.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term concerning data access or use is unfair within the meaning of Article 13 if it grossly deviates from good commercial practice in data access and use, contrary to the requirements of good faith and fair dealing.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot include a contractual term that excludes liability for intentional acts or gross negligence — such a term is conclusively unfair and not binding.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term that excludes liability for intentional acts or gross negligence is conclusively deemed unfair and is not binding on the party on whom it was unilaterally imposed.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot include a contractual term that eliminates remedies for non-performance — such a term is conclusively unfair and not binding.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term that eliminates all remedies available to the non-imposing party in the event of non-performance of contractual obligations is conclusively deemed unfair and not binding.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: You cannot include a contractual term that grants one party exclusive rights to determine the meaning of the contract — such a term is conclusively unfair and not binding.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term that grants one contracting party the exclusive right to interpret the terms and conditions of the contract is conclusively deemed unfair and not binding on the other party.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: A contractual term that inappropriately limits remedies or extends liability beyond what is commercially reasonable is presumed unfair unless the imposing party proves otherwise.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term that inappropriately limits the remedies available to the non-imposing party or extends the liability of that party beyond what is commercially reasonable is presumptively unfair, subject to rebuttal by the imposing party.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: A contractual term that allows detrimental access to commercially sensitive information of the other party is presumed unfair unless rebutted.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term that permits the imposing party to access commercially sensitive information of the other party in a manner that is detrimental to the latter's interests is presumptively unfair.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: A contractual term that prevents a party from using data provided under the contract is presumed unfair unless rebutted.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term that prevents the non-imposing party from using data made available under the contract is presumptively unfair, subject to rebuttal.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Data Act (European Union, 2023-12-13).

rule_text: A contractual term that restricts termination rights or prevents data copying is presumed unfair unless rebutted.
rule_text_technical: A contractual term that restricts the termination rights of the non-imposing party or prevents that party from making copies of data provided under the contract is presumptively unfair.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)

rule_text: Organizations should establish, implement, maintain, and continually improve an Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS) in accordance with the requirements of this standard.

first_instance.law_name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI Management System (ISO/IEC, 2023-12-18).

Both rules recommend implementing foundational AI governance structures before applying supplementary guidance, but this rule specifically addresses the sequencing relationship between AI RMF 1.0 and the GenAI profile AI 600-1, whereas the existing rule concerns establishing an AIMS per ISO 42001.

Both require establishing, implementing, maintaining, and documenting a structured program (AIMS vs. cybersecurity program), but Ontario Bill 194 is a binding statute focused specifically on cybersecurity governance and risk for public sector entities, while ISO 42001 is a voluntary AI management system standard with broader AI scope.

instances.citation: Principle 4 — Accountability and Governance (regulator guidance — governance requirements)
instances.notes: Both address governance requirements including oversight, documentation, and audit trails for AI systems, but the UK White Paper provides non-binding guidance directed at regulators on what to consider, whereas ISO 42001 sets out a structured management system framework for organizations to implement.

Both recommend structuring AI risk management programs around a defined framework with governance functions, but the DHS rule specifically references the four NIST AI RMF functions for critical infrastructure contexts, while ISO 42001 establishes a comprehensive AI Management System framework.

Both advocate a comprehensive governance approach integrating technology and management across the AI chain, but this rule explicitly names all parties in the AI supply chain as responsible, whereas ISO 42001 focuses on establishing a management system within a single organization.

rule_text: Organizations should determine and document the scope of their AIMS, including the boundaries and applicability of the management system.
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that the organization determine the boundaries and applicability of the AI management system to establish its scope, which shall be available as documented information.

rule_text: Top management should review the organization's AIMS at planned intervals to ensure its continuing suitability, adequacy, effectiveness, and alignment with the organization's strategic direction.
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that top management review the organization's AI management system at planned intervals to ensure its continuing suitability, adequacy and effectiveness, considering changes in external and internal issues, AI performance information, and opportunities for continual improvement.

first_instance.law_name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)

Both require post-deployment review of AI system performance, but the ISO rule is a voluntary management system standard for top management review of the AIMS, while this is a binding legal obligation specifically targeting high-stakes AI applications and explicitly including fairness evaluation.

Both require organizations to maintain accountability and internal governance for AI systems, but the ISO rule focuses on management review of an AIMS at planned intervals, while this guideline is a broader voluntary recommendation about accountability for AI impacts and governance structures.

rule_text: Organizations should react to nonconformities related to the AIMS, take action to control and correct them, investigate causes, and implement corrective actions to prevent recurrence.
rule_text_technical: It is recommended that the organization, when a nonconformity occurs, react to the nonconformity, evaluate the need for action to eliminate the causes of the nonconformity, implement any action needed, review the effectiveness of any corrective action taken, and make changes to the AI management system if necessary.

rule_text: You cannot distribute or cause to be distributed any political advertisement or campaign communication containing a materially deceptive AI-generated depiction of a candidate for public office or a current public official within 90 days before any New Mexico primary, general, or special election.
rule_text_technical: No person or entity may distribute or cause to be distributed any political advertisement or campaign communication that contains a materially deceptive AI-generated depiction of a candidate for public office or a current public official, where 'materially deceptive' means the AI-generated content depicts the candidate or official saying, doing, or appearing in a manner that did not occur and that is likely to deceive a reasonable viewer, within the 90-day period preceding any New Mexico primary, general, or special election.

Both Indiana and New Mexico independently prohibit distributing materially deceptive AI-generated content in political advertising, but are drafted differently and may vary in specific thresholds or scope.

instances.citation: Key Provisions § 1 (Prohibition on Materially Deceptive AI-Generated Media)
instances.notes: Both prohibit distribution of materially deceptive AI-generated political content but Alabama's rule emphasizes the 'reasonable viewer' standard for deception about a candidate's statements or conduct, while New Mexico's framing differs in structure and scope.

Both prohibit distributing deceptive AI-generated/synthetic media in political contexts, but Arizona focuses on 'deepfakes of a candidate or political party' with a knowledge requirement, while New Mexico broadly covers 'materially deceptive AI-generated political content' without restricting to deepfakes of candidates.
Both prohibit distribution of materially deceptive AI-generated content involving candidates, but Nevada adds a specific 60-day pre-election temporal window not present in New Mexico's rule.

Both Hawaii Act 191 and New Mexico HB 182 prohibit distributing materially deceptive AI-generated media depicting candidates or officials in an electoral context, but Hawaii's law specifies a temporal window tied to elections and is drafted independently with different scope and phrasing.

Both prohibit publishing/distributing AI-generated or digitally manipulated content in election advertising, but Singapore's rule targets online election advertising specifically and uses 'digitally generated or digitally altered' framing, while the New Mexico rule focuses on 'materially deceptive AI-generated' political content without the online-specific scope.

Both prohibit use of AI/synthetic media in political/electioneering communications without disclosure, but Kentucky creates civil liability for non-disclosure while New Mexico focuses on prohibiting materially deceptive content distribution.

instances.citation: Key Provisions — Prohibition on Unlabeled Election Deepfakes
instances.notes: Both prohibit distributing AI-generated/deceptive political content to influence elections, but SD SB164 uses a specific 90-day window and focuses on unlabeled deepfakes rather than broadly 'materially deceptive' content, and NM requires a disclaimer rather than an outright prohibition on unlabeled content.

Both prohibit distributing materially deceptive AI-generated content in political/campaign communications, but Rhode Island H5872 uses 'campaign communication' and specifies a temporal window ('within'), while NM HB182 uses 'political advertisement or campaign communication' without the same temporal framing.

rule_text: You cannot distribute materially deceptive AI-generated political content through any channel, including broadcast, cable, print, digital, social media, or direct mail, when targeting New Mexico voters.

Both rules authorize the Attorney General to bring civil enforcement actions for violations, but the California rule specifies a fixed $5,000 per-violation civil penalty while the New Mexico rule focuses on injunctive relief and unspecified civil penalties.

instances.notes: Both prohibit producing, distributing, and possessing CSAM including AI/computer-generated depictions of minors in sexually explicit conduct, but Iowa SF 2243 focuses on filming/photographing/recording acts involving real or depicted minors while Pennsylvania Act 125 explicitly extends the prohibition to AI-generated and computer-generated images under a broader verb set (produce, distribute, disseminate, possess, control).

Both prohibit creating sexual or nude depictions of real identifiable minors, but Wyoming's rule is specific to AI-generated synthetic vocal or visual representations, while Iowa's rule covers filming, photographing, or recording more broadly without an AI-specific focus.

Both prohibit creation of child sexual abuse material including AI-generated or digitally altered depictions of minors, but Iowa SF2243 is broader (covering filming, photographing, recording) while SC Act 57 specifically targets obscene visual representations including AI-generated CSAM.

rule_text: The prohibition on child sexual abuse material expressly covers images and depictions that are digitally created or digitally altered, meaning AI-generated or deepfake imagery of minors in sexual contexts is covered even if no actual minor was used in production.
rule_text_technical: The term 'digitally created or digitally altered' as used in the amended Iowa Code § 728.12 encompasses any image, photograph, film, or depiction produced or modified through digital means, including through the use of artificial intelligence, to portray a minor engaged in a sex act or in a state of nudity, regardless of whether an actual minor participated in the creation of the original material.
