rule_text: You must include a prominent, clearly legible or audible disclosure stating that the content was generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence in any AI-generated content used in political advertising or political communications.
rule_text_technical: Any AI-generated content used in political advertising or political communications must include a prominent, clearly legible or audible disclosure stating that the content was generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence.

first_instance.law_name: Alabama House Bill 172 — Prohibition on Materially Deceptive AI-Generated Media in Elections

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Alabama HB 172 (AI Election Deepfakes) (Alabama, 2024-04-24).

Both require public disclosure about AI systems, but Colorado's rule targets developers of high-risk AI systems and requires a summary statement about types developed, whereas Alabama's rule focuses on disclosure of AI-generated content in political advertising.

Both require a visible warning/disclosure on potentially harmful AI-generated or regulated content, but the French rule targets pornographic content simulating crimes with criminal sanctions, while the Alabama rule targets AI-generated political content with a different scope and enforcement mechanism.

Both rules concern disclosure of AI-altered or AI-generated content to audiences, but Arizona HB 2394 frames the requirement as an element of a civil cause of action (plaintiff must prove absence of disclosure to prevail), whereas Alabama HB172 directly mandates a prominent disclosure as an affirmative obligation on the publisher.

Both Nevada and Alabama require a clear and conspicuous AI-disclosure disclaimer on politically-related AI-generated or manipulated content, but Nevada specifies exact disclaimer language and format requirements while Alabama's text is more general.

Both Hawaii Act 191 and Alabama HB172 require a prominent disclosure identifying AI-generated content in political advertising, but they were independently drafted with different phrasing, scope details, and state-specific contexts.

Both require a clear and conspicuous disclosure that content was generated or substantially altered using AI in political/election communications, but NC uses a specific prescribed disclosure phrase and is scoped to election communications depicting real candidates or elected officials, while AL HB172 applies more broadly to political advertising.

Both require a prominent disclosure label on political/election content that has been digitally generated or altered using AI, but Singapore's rule is specific to online election advertising and mandates an 'AI disclosure label' rather than a general audible/legible disclosure statement, and is administered by an Elections Department rather than a general political advertising regulator.

Both require prominent, clear AI-generated content disclosures using standardized language, but China's GB45438-2025 is a binding technical standard specifying labeling of synthetic content broadly with standardized expressions, while Alabama HB172 targets political advertising specifically and focuses on material deception context.

Both SD SB164 and AL HB172 require a prominent disclaimer on AI-generated content depicting real persons in political contexts, but they are drafted differently and may differ in scope, threshold, or specific wording of the required disclaimer.

Both require a prominent disclosure that content was AI-generated in political communications, but North Dakota specifies the exact disclaimer text 'This content generated by artificial intelligence.' while Alabama requires disclosure of 'generated or substantially altered using artificial intelligence' without mandating a verbatim phrase.

Both require a prominent, clearly legible or audible disclosure that content was generated or substantially altered using AI in political advertising, but Rhode Island specifies the exact disclosure language while Alabama's rule is more general.

Both rules require a label/disclosure to be attached to AI-generated or AI-altered content, but Singapore's rule is regulator-directed (Commissioner issues a labelling direction to specific communicators/administrators) rather than a general self-disclosure obligation on all producers of AI content, and applies in an online safety context rather than a political advertising context.

Both concern a disclosure standard for AI-generated content, but this rule is a voluntary executive order recommendation to initiate FCC rulemaking for a uniform federal standard, whereas us-al-hb172-2024 is a binding state law mandating a specific disclosure in political advertising.

rule_text: You can be charged with a Class C felony, punishable by one to ten years in state prison, for any subsequent violation of this law occurring within five years of a first violation.
rule_text_technical: A subsequent violation of the prohibition occurring within five years of the first violation is elevated to a Class C felony, punishable by one to ten years in state prison.

Both rules are from Alabama 2024 AI-image laws imposing criminal penalties, but HB172 addresses subsequent felony offenses while HB161 addresses first-offense misdemeanor liability for nonconsensual AI-generated intimate images, making them complementary rather than identical in scope and severity.

Both rules establish enhanced felony penalties for subsequent/repeat offenses, but Alabama's rule specifies a Class C felony for violations within five years (1–10 years imprisonment) while North Dakota's rule specifies a Class C felony for any subsequent offense with up to 5 years imprisonment and a fine up to $10,000, covering different subject matter (deepfakes vs. unspecified) and different sentencing ranges.

Both rules criminalize AI-related conduct as felonies, but Pennsylvania's Act 35 targets AI-generated fake content used for fraud (third-degree felony) while Alabama's HB172 targets subsequent violations within a five-year window and specifies Class C felony with 1–10 year imprisonment, making the subject matter, triggering conduct, and penalty structure meaningfully different.

Both laws impose felony-level criminal penalties for AI-generated nonconsensual intimate image offenses, but SD SB 41 sets a single tier of up to 5 years imprisonment and $10,000 fine per count, whereas Alabama HB172 specifies a Class C felony for subsequent violations with 1–10 years imprisonment, reflecting different penalty structures and triggering conditions.

rule_text: You do not violate the prohibition on materially deceptive media if your political advertising uses AI-generated content but includes proper, required disclosure.

Both laws prohibit non-consensual dissemination of AI-generated sexually explicit images of identifiable individuals, but Louisiana's statute adds a specific criminal intent element (coerce, harass, intimidate, or maliciously harm) and is a criminal statute rather than a civil one, distinguishing it meaningfully from Alabama's HB161.

rule_text: When establishing profits from unauthorized use, the injured party need only prove gross revenue attributable to the use, while the violator bears the burden of proving deductible expenses.
rule_text_technical: In establishing profits, the injured party or parties shall be required to present proof only of the gross revenue attributable to the use, and the person who violated the section shall prove the person's deductible expenses.

rule_text: You cannot use the expressive works exemption to shield a direct commercial use of a deceased personality's likeness within an otherwise exempt work if that use constitutes advertising, selling, or soliciting purchases of a product or service.
rule_text_technical: If a work described in clause (i) includes within it a use in connection with a product, article of merchandise, good, or service, this use shall not be exempt under this subparagraph, notwithstanding the unprotected use's inclusion in a work otherwise exempt, if the claimant proves that this use is so directly connected with a product, article of merchandise, good, or service as to constitute an act of advertising, selling, or soliciting purchases of that product, article of merchandise, good, or service by the deceased personality without prior consent.

Both rules restrict a specific carve-out that would otherwise permit use of a deceased performer's likeness without full consent, but CA AB1836 addresses the expressive works exemption for commercial use while NY SB8391 addresses the disclaimer carve-out as a substitute for estate/authorized-representative consent.

rule_text: You are liable for a minimum of $10,000 or actual damages for producing, distributing, or making available an unauthorized digital replica of a deceased personality in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording.
rule_text_technical: A person who produces, distributes, or makes available the digital replica of a deceased personality's voice or likeness in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording without prior consent shall be liable to any injured party in an amount equal to the greater of ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or the actual damages suffered by a person controlling the rights to the deceased personality's likeness.

rule_text: You may use a digital replica of a deceased personality without consent if the use is fleeting or incidental.

rule_text: The rights of a deceased personality under this section are freely transferable property rights that may be transferred or inherited by contract, trust, or testamentary instrument, and any contract entered into by the deceased personality during their lifetime assigning these rights remains valid and enforceable.
rule_text_technical: The rights recognized under this section are property rights, freely transferable or descendible, in whole or in part, by contract or by means of any trust or any other testamentary instrument, executed before or after January 1, 1985; the rights shall be deemed to have existed at the time of death of any deceased personality who died prior to January 1, 1985; nothing in this section shall be construed to render invalid or unenforceable any contract entered into by a deceased personality during their lifetime by which the deceased personality assigned the rights, in whole or in part, to use the deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness.

rule_text: After the death of a personality, rights under this section vest in surviving family members in a defined order of priority: surviving spouse and/or children and grandchildren first, then surviving parents if no spouse or descendants exist; rights may be exercised by those holding in aggregate more than a one-half interest.
rule_text_technical: After the death of any person, the rights under this section shall belong to the following person or persons and may be exercised, on behalf of and for the benefit of all of those persons, by those persons who, in the aggregate, are entitled to more than a one-half interest in the rights: (1) surviving spouse unless there are surviving children or grandchildren, in which case one-half belongs to the surviving spouse; (2) surviving children and grandchildren unless there is a surviving spouse; (3) if no surviving spouse, children, or grandchildren, then surviving parent or parents; (4) children's and grandchildren's rights are divided and exercisable per Section 240 of the Probate Code.

first_instance.law_name: Use of Digital Replicas of Deceased Performers Act

rule_text: If a deceased personality did not transfer their rights by contract, trust, or testamentary instrument and no surviving family members as described in the succession provisions exist, the rights under this section shall terminate.
rule_text_technical: If any deceased personality does not transfer the deceased personality's rights under this section by contract, or by means of a trust or testamentary instrument, and there are no surviving persons as described in subdivision (d), then the rights set forth in subdivision (a) shall terminate.

rule_text: You cannot enforce a contractual provision that allows use of a digital replica of an individual's voice or likeness in place of in-person work if that provision meets all three specified conditions relating to description of uses and lack of legal or union representation.
rule_text_technical: A provision in an agreement between an individual and any other person for the performance of personal or professional services is unenforceable only as it relates to a new performance, fixed on or after January 1, 2025, by a digital replica of the individual if the provision: (1) allows for the creation and use of a digital replica of the individual's voice or likeness in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person; (2) does not include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica (subject to exception); and (3) the individual was not represented by qualifying legal counsel or a labor union whose collective bargaining agreement expressly addresses digital replica uses.

rule_text: A contractual provision is unenforceable if it allows a digital replica of an individual's voice or likeness to substitute for work the individual would otherwise have performed in person.
rule_text_technical: Unenforceability attaches where the provision allows for the creation and use of a digital replica of the individual's voice or likeness in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person, provided the other conditions in subdivision (a) are also met.

rule_text: You must include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of a digital replica in a contract provision, or that provision risks being unenforceable.
rule_text_technical: Except as provided in subparagraph (B), failure to include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica in a contractual provision is a condition that renders the provision unenforceable under subdivision (a).

rule_text: A contract provision is not unenforceable solely for lacking a specific description of digital replica uses, if those uses are consistent with the terms of the contract and the fundamental character of the photography or soundtrack as recorded or performed.
rule_text_technical: Failure to include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of a digital replica does not render the provision unenforceable if the uses are consistent with the terms of the contract for the performance of personal or professional services and the fundamental character of the photography or soundtrack as recorded or performed.

rule_text: A digital replica contract provision is enforceable if the individual was represented by legal counsel who negotiated the licensing of the individual's digital replica rights and the commercial terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in a signed or initialed writing.
rule_text_technical: The provision is not rendered unenforceable under subdivision (a)(3) if the individual was represented by legal counsel who negotiated on behalf of the individual licensing the individual's digital replica rights, and the commercial terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in a contract or other writing signed or initialed by the individual.

rule_text_technical: The provision is not rendered unenforceable under subdivision (a)(3) if the individual is represented by a labor union representing workers who do the proposed work, and the terms of their collective bargaining agreement expressly addresses uses of digital replicas.

rule_text: The unenforceability of a digital replica provision does not affect other provisions of the same contract, and does not impact any exclusivity grants contained in or related to that provision.
rule_text_technical: Section 927 does not affect provisions of a contract other than a provision that falls under subdivision (a) and does not impact, abrogate, or otherwise affect any exclusivity grants contained in, or related to, a provision subject to subdivision (a).

rule_text: Electronic reproduction, sampling, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering of a sound recording or audiovisual work authorized by the copyright holder is excluded from the definition of 'digital replica' and is not subject to this law.
rule_text_technical: 'Digital replica' does not include the electronic reproduction, use of a sample of one sound recording or audiovisual work into another, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering of a sound recording or audiovisual work authorized by the copyright holder.

rule_text: You must make available, at no cost to users, an AI detection tool that allows users to assess whether image, video, or audio content was created or altered by your GenAI system, outputs system provenance data, withholds personal provenance data, is publicly accessible, accepts content uploads or URLs, and supports an API.
rule_text_technical: A covered provider shall make available an AI detection tool at no cost to the user that: (1) allows a user to assess whether image, video, or audio content was created or altered by the covered provider's GenAI system; (2) outputs any system provenance data detected in the content; (3) does not output any personal provenance data detected in the content; (4) is publicly accessible (subject to reasonable security limitations); (5) allows content upload or URL submission; and (6) supports an API allowing invocation without visiting the covered provider's website.

first_instance.law_name: California AI Transparency Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California SB 942 (AI Transparency Act) (California, 2024-09-19).
This rule is a near-verbatim restatement of the SB 942 detection tool requirement, incorporated into AB 853 as a technical correction without substantive change to the underlying obligation.

Both laws address manifest/visible disclosure of AI-generated content, but California SB 942 focuses on providing a detection tool to users while Washington's rule imposes an affirmative obligation on providers to offer users the option to embed a visible disclosure directly in the content.

rule_text: You may impose reasonable limitations on access to your AI detection tool only to prevent or respond to demonstrable risks to the security or integrity of your GenAI system.
rule_text_technical: A covered provider may impose reasonable limitations on access to the AI detection tool to prevent, or respond to, demonstrable risks to the security or integrity of its GenAI system, as an exception to the public accessibility requirement.

rule_text: You must collect user feedback on the efficacy of your AI detection tool and incorporate relevant feedback into efforts to improve the tool.
rule_text_technical: A covered provider shall collect user feedback related to the efficacy of the covered provider's AI detection tool and incorporate relevant feedback into any attempt to improve the efficacy of the tool.

first_instance.law_name: California AI Transparency Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California SB 942 (AI Transparency Act) (California, 2024-09-19).

rule_text: You cannot collect or retain personal information from users of your AI detection tool, except in the limited opt-in feedback contact scenario.
rule_text_technical: A covered provider shall not collect or retain personal information from users of the covered provider's AI detection tool, except as provided in the opt-in contact information exception under § 22757.2(c)(1)(B).

rule_text: If you discover that a third-party licensee has modified your licensed GenAI system such that it can no longer include the required latent disclosure, you must revoke the license within 96 hours of that discovery.
rule_text_technical: If a covered provider knows that a third-party licensee modified a licensed GenAI system such that it is no longer capable of including a disclosure required by subdivision (b) in content the system creates or alters, the covered provider shall revoke the license within 96 hours of discovering the licensee's action.

This rule is functionally identical to the California SB 942 provision requiring covered providers to revoke a licensee's license upon discovering that the licensee modified the system so it can no longer include the required latent disclosure.

Both rules address the allocation of liability between AI developers/providers and third-party operators/licensees who misuse or modify a system, but the Idaho rule provides a blanket developer liability shield for third-party operator violations, while the California rule focuses narrowly on the specific scenario of license revocation after unauthorized modification that disables required disclosures.

rule_text: As a third-party licensee, you must cease using a licensed GenAI system once the covered provider has revoked your license pursuant to the modification prohibition.
rule_text_technical: A third-party licensee shall cease using a licensed GenAI system after the license for the system has been revoked by the covered provider pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (c) of Section 22757.3.

rule_text: A prevailing plaintiff in an enforcement action under this chapter is entitled to recover all reasonable attorney's costs and fees.
rule_text_technical: A prevailing plaintiff in an action brought pursuant to subdivision (a)(1) shall be entitled to all reasonable attorney's costs and fees.

rule_text_technical: For a violation by a third-party licensee of paragraph (3) of subdivision (c) of Section 22757.3, the Attorney General, a county counsel, or a city attorney may bring a civil action for injunctive relief and reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

Code §22757 et seq.), but SB 942 targets third-party licensees violating GenAI licensing requirements while TFAIA imposes broader civil penalties for noncompliance with frontier AI transparency obligations.

Both California laws allow sub-state government attorneys (city attorneys and county counsel) to bring enforcement actions, but SB 942 addresses GenAI system licensing violations while AB 489 addresses healthcare AI deception, and the enforcement actors and triggers differ meaningfully.

Both rules concern civil enforcement of AI detection tool and disclosure requirements under California law (AB 853 incorporating SB 942), but the new rule specifies a $5,000 per-violation civil penalty structure while the existing rule addresses the specific scenario of a third-party licensee's failure to cease using a revoked licensed GenAI system with different enforcement actors.

rule_text: This chapter does not apply to products, services, websites, or applications that provide exclusively non-user-generated video game, television, streaming, movie, or interactive experiences.
rule_text_technical: This chapter does not apply to any product, service, internet website, or application that provides exclusively non-user-generated video game, television, streaming, movie, or interactive experiences.

rule_text: You must include in your posted documentation a high-level summary of the datasets used in developing your generative AI system or service, covering all specified elements.
rule_text_technical: The documentation required under § 3111 must include, at minimum, a high-level summary of the datasets used in the development of the generative artificial intelligence system or service, encompassing all elements enumerated in § 3111(a)(1) through (12).

Both rules require disclosure of training dataset information, but the Connecticut rule is a non-binding recommendation to publish on a website or in product documentation, whereas California AB 2013 imposes a binding mandate to post a high-level summary of datasets used in developing generative AI systems.

Both California laws require public website publication of AI-related documentation, but this rule applies specifically to 'frontier models' and mandates a broader 'frontier AI framework' rather than dataset-focused documentation under AB 2013.

rule_text: Your dataset documentation must describe how the datasets further the intended purpose of your AI system or service.
rule_text_technical: The high-level summary of datasets required under § 3111(a) must include a description of how the datasets further the intended purpose of the artificial intelligence system or service.

rule_text_technical: The high-level summary of datasets required under § 3111(a) must include the number of data points included in the datasets, which may be in general ranges, and with estimated figures for dynamic datasets.

rule_text: You are not required to post training data documentation if your generative AI system or service is solely dedicated to security and integrity purposes.

rule_text: All references in Pennsylvania's Prisons and Parole statutes to 'child pornography' are replaced with 'child sexual abuse material,' and this updated terminology governs all relevant criminal and parole-related proceedings.
rule_text_technical: Act 125 of 2024 makes editorial amendments to Title 61 (Prisons and Parole) of the Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes to replace all references to the term 'child pornography' with the term 'child sexual abuse material,' ensuring terminological consistency with the amended criminal offenses provisions and applicable to all proceedings, classifications, and determinations governed by Title 61.

rule_text: You cannot create, distribute, publish, or cause to be distributed or published a deceptive AI-generated advertisement concerning any candidate or elected official within 90 days of an election unless the advertisement includes the required disclaimer.
rule_text_technical: It is unlawful for any person to create, distribute, publish, or cause to be distributed or published a deceptive AI-generated advertisement concerning any candidate or elected official within 90 days of an election, unless the advertisement includes the required disclaimer as specified in subsection (b).

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina Protecting Elections from Deceptive AI Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina SB 815 (AI in Elections) (North Carolina, 2024-10-03).

Both rules prohibit publishing deceptive AI-generated election advertisements depicting candidates falsely, but the Singapore Act is framed as a general online election advertising prohibition with a fabrication/substantially false standard, while the NC rule specifically targets 'deceptive AI-generated advertisement concerning any candidate or election' with slightly different scope and drafting.

Both prohibit assisting in the creation or distribution of AI-generated content designed to deceive, but the NC rule is narrowly scoped to electoral/candidate advertising while this Chinese standard broadly covers all AI-generated synthetic content across any context, and imposes the obligation on service providers rather than content creators.

instances.citation: Obligations for Generative AI Service Providers — Prohibition on Generating Certain Content, ¶2
instances.notes: Both prohibit AI-generated deceptive content involving electoral candidates during electoral periods, but the India rule targets generative AI service providers producing impersonating synthetic media, while the NC rule targets creators and distributors of deceptive AI-generated political advertisements.

instances.citation: Law No. 5651 Amendment — BTK Emergency Blocking Powers (§ Election Disinformation)
instances.notes: Both prohibit AI-generated election disinformation/deceptive AI content related to elections, but Turkey's rule adds a state administrative blocking mechanism (BTK emergency order) absent from the US provision, and differs in scope and enforcement structure.

rule_text: You cannot create or distribute a materially deceptive AI-generated depiction of a candidate casting a ballot, operating a voting machine, or performing any act related to the casting of a ballot.
rule_text_technical: It is unlawful for any person to create or distribute a materially deceptive AI-generated depiction of a candidate casting a ballot, operating a voting machine, or performing any act related to the casting of a ballot, with no time or disclaimer exception provided for this specific prohibition.

first_instance.law_name: North Carolina Protecting Elections from Deceptive AI Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in North Carolina SB 815 (AI in Elections) (North Carolina, 2024-10-03).

Both rules prohibit using AI-generated representations to falsely depict candidates in election contexts, but the Singapore Act focuses on impersonation via voice/facial synthesis in online election advertising broadly, while the NC rule specifically targets depictions of candidates performing voting or election-related acts.

instances.citation: Law No. 5651 Amendment — BTK Emergency Blocking Powers (§ Impersonation of Public Officials)
instances.notes: Both prohibit AI-generated content impersonating candidates/public officials in ways likely to mislead voters, but Turkey's rule encompasses a broader category of public officials (not limited to candidates performing electoral acts) and adds BTK emergency blocking enforcement.

Both Hawaii Act 191 and North Carolina SB815 prohibit distributing materially deceptive AI-generated depictions related to candidates or elections, but they differ in drafting, specific scope (Hawaii covers political parties and elected officials broadly; NC focuses on specific voting-related conduct), and jurisdictional context.

Both prohibit AI-generated/digitally altered deceptive depictions of real persons, but PA Act 35 targets non-consensual forged digital likenesses (deepfakes, voice clones) with intent to deceive broadly, while NC SB815 is narrowly scoped to electoral candidates and voting-related conduct.

rule_text: You must remove a deceptive AI-generated election communication within 48 hours of receiving actual notice from the depicted candidate, elected official, or political party, or you may be subject to civil liability under Section 2.
rule_text_technical: Any online platform that receives actual notice of a deceptive AI-generated election communication in violation of this Article and fails to remove it within 48 hours of receiving notice from the depicted candidate, elected official, or political party may be subject to civil liability as set out in Section 2.

rule_text: You must use the term 'data controller' (not 'data user') when referring to entities that process personal data, except where specifically provided otherwise.
rule_text_technical: The principal Act is amended by substituting 'data user' and 'data users' wherever appearing with 'data controller' and 'data controllers', except in the definition of 'register' under section 4 and in section 9.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: You must treat biometric data — personal data resulting from technical processing relating to physical, physiological, or behavioural characteristics — as a defined category of personal data under the Act.
rule_text_technical: The term 'biometric data' is defined as any personal data resulting from technical processing relating to the physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a person.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: You must treat any breach, loss, misuse, or unauthorised access of personal data as a 'personal data breach' under the Act.
rule_text_technical: The term 'personal data breach' is defined as any breach of personal data, loss of personal data, misuse of personal data or unauthorized access of personal data.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: You cannot extend data subject rights to deceased individuals, as deceased persons are excluded from the definition of 'data subject' under the Act.
rule_text_technical: The definition of 'data subject' is amended to expressly exclude deceased individuals from its scope.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: You cannot rely on the appointment of a data protection officer to discharge your own duties and functions under the Act — those responsibilities remain with you as data controller or data processor.
rule_text_technical: The appointment of a data protection officer does not discharge the data controller or data processor from any duties and functions under this Act.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: You are only required to fulfil a data portability request subject to technical feasibility and compatibility of the data format.
rule_text_technical: The right to data portability is subject to the technical feasibility and compatibility of the data format between the transmitting and receiving data controllers.

first_instance.law_name: Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act A1727)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Malaysia PDPA Amendment 2024 (Malaysia, 2024-10-09).

rule_text: You may serve documents under the Act by electronic means, as electronic service is now an expressly authorised mode of service.
rule_text_technical: Service of documents by electronic means is expressly permitted as an authorised mode of service under section 136 of the Act.

rule_text: You must ensure that all products with digital elements are designed and developed in accordance with the essential cybersecurity requirements laid down in this Regulation, including both physically and logically connected products.
rule_text_technical: Manufacturers shall ensure that all products with digital elements, whether connected physically via hardware interfaces or logically via network sockets, pipes, files, APIs, or any other software interface, are designed and developed in accordance with the essential cybersecurity requirements established by this Regulation.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must ensure that your product's integrated remote data processing solutions meet cybersecurity requirements under this Regulation, where such remote processing is necessary for the product to perform one of its functions.
rule_text_technical: Remote data processing solutions designed and developed by or on behalf of the manufacturer, the absence of which would prevent the product with digital elements from performing one of its functions, fall within the scope of this Regulation and must comply with its cybersecurity requirements.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must take cybersecurity into account throughout supply chains, ensuring that final products with digital elements and their components are secure.
rule_text_technical: Cybersecurity requirements under this Regulation apply throughout supply chains, requiring that final products with digital elements and their constituent components satisfy the applicable cybersecurity requirements, thereby making the entire supply chain more secure.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must ensure the cybersecurity of products with digital elements that are only indirectly connected to other devices or networks, as cyber threats can propagate through multiple products via chained vulnerability exploits.
rule_text_technical: Manufacturers shall ensure the cybersecurity of products with digital elements that are only indirectly connected to other devices or networks, given that cyber threats may propagate through various products with digital elements by chaining together multiple vulnerability exploits before reaching a target.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must comply with objective-oriented and technology-neutral essential cybersecurity requirements that apply horizontally to all products with digital elements placed on the internal market.
rule_text_technical: All products with digital elements placed on the Union internal market must conform to objective-oriented and technology-neutral essential cybersecurity requirements that apply horizontally, as introduced by this Regulation to increase the overall level of cybersecurity.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must comply with a harmonised Union regulatory framework of cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, replacing the fragmented patchwork of national and sectoral measures.
rule_text_technical: Economic operators and manufacturers are subject to a single harmonised horizontal Union regulatory framework establishing comprehensive cybersecurity requirements for all products with digital elements, superseding the previous legislative patchwork of national and sectoral measures and ensuring legal certainty across the internal market.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: The Commission should provide guidance to assist economic operators, particularly microenterprises and SMEs, on the scope of this Regulation including remote data processing, free and open-source software, support period criteria, interplay with other Union law, and the concept of substantial modification.
rule_text_technical: The Commission shall provide guidance to assist economic operators, in particular microenterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises, covering the scope of this Regulation including remote data processing implications for free and open-source software developers, criteria for determining support periods, interplay with other Union law, and the concept of substantial modification.

first_instance.law_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Cyber Resilience Act (2024) (European Union, 2024-10-10).

rule_text: You must apply all provisions of the Annex to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC in their entirety, including rules on partner and linked enterprises, when determining whether your enterprise qualifies as a microenterprise or SME under this Regulation.
rule_text_technical: When determining the category an enterprise falls into for the purposes of this Regulation, the provisions of the Annex to Recommendation 2003/361/EC shall be applied in their entirety, including Article 6 on establishing data of an enterprise in consideration of partner enterprises or linked enterprises, for calculating staff headcount and financial ceilings.

rule_text: You must ensure the AI disclosure obligation applies to any AI-generated content depicting a candidate that is re-published or shared during the election period, even if that content was originally created before the election period began.
rule_text_technical: The disclosure obligation for AI-generated content applies to content published during the election period (Nomination Day to Polling Day), regardless of when it was created. Content created before the election period that depicts a candidate and is re-published or shared during the election period is required to include the mandatory AI disclosure label.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

Both establish a temporal election-period window for AI-generated content obligations, but SD SB164 specifies a fixed 90-day pre-election window for state/county/municipal elections while Singapore's EIOA ties obligations to the official election period for candidate-depicting content.

rule_text: Online platforms must remove or apply the required AI disclosure label to non-compliant AI-generated election advertising within 24 hours of receiving a notice from the Returning Officer.
rule_text_technical: Online platforms that host user-generated content used as election advertising must remove or apply the required disclosure label to AI-generated election advertising within 24 hours of receiving a take-down or correction direction notice from the Returning Officer.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

Both rules require digital platforms to remove non-compliant AI-generated content within 48 hours of notice, but the Colombian rule targets non-consensual intimate imagery while the Singaporean rule targets non-compliant AI-generated election advertising.

Both rules impose compliance obligations on recipients of directions to cease or remove online material in Singapore, but this rule targets individual communicators via a stop communication direction while the EIOA rule targets platforms removing non-compliant AI-generated election advertising.

instances.citation: Law No. 5651 Amendment — 6-Hour Takedown Obligation (§ Escalating Penalties)
instances.notes: Both impose short mandatory compliance windows (24 hours vs 6 hours) for platform action on AI-generated content with escalating consequences for non-compliance, but Turkey's rule adds escalating fines and platform blocking orders beyond Singapore's labelling/takedown framework.

rule_text: The Returning Officer may issue take-down notices, correction direction orders, refer cases to the police, and apply to court for urgent injunctive relief against publishers of non-compliant AI-generated election advertising.
rule_text_technical: The Returning Officer is empowered to: (1) issue take-down notices to publishers of non-compliant AI-generated election advertising; (2) issue correction direction orders requiring publishers to add the required disclosure label; (3) refer cases to the police for investigation and prosecution; and (4) apply to court for urgent injunctive relief to prevent continued publication of non-compliant content.

first_instance.law_name: Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act 2024 (Singapore)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Singapore Elections (AI Integrity) Act 2024 (Singapore, 2024-10-15).

Both rules grant a Singapore Commissioner/Returning Officer powers to issue directions to parties inside and outside Singapore following a report or complaint, but the OSARA rule is broader in scope (online safety content) and applies to a wider range of subjects than the election-advertising-specific EIOA rule.

instances.citation: Law No. 5651 Amendment — BTK Emergency Blocking Powers (§ Administrative Blocking Without Court Order)
instances.notes: Both grant a regulatory authority emergency powers to restrict platform access to AI-generated content without waiting for full proceedings, but Turkey's BTK rule explicitly bypasses prior court authorisation while Singapore's Returning Officer powers include court-applied injunctive relief as one option.

rule_text: You must apply no-fault liability rules to all movables, including software, whether integrated into other movables or installed in immovables.
rule_text_technical: No-fault liability for defective products shall apply to all movables, including software, irrespective of whether they are integrated into other movables or installed in immovables, in order to ensure a comprehensive Union product liability regime.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

Both define the scope of a EU civil liability instrument covering AI/software products, but this Directive targets non-contractual civil liability specifically for AI systems across all risk classifications, whereas the PLD covers no-fault liability for all products including software more broadly.

rule_text: You cannot apply this Directive's liability rules to damage arising from nuclear accidents where liability for such damage is covered by international conventions ratified by Member States.
rule_text_technical: Liability for defective products shall not apply to damage arising from nuclear accidents in so far as liability for such damage is covered by international conventions ratified by Member States.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You must treat software — including AI systems, operating systems, firmware, applications, and software-as-a-service — as a 'product' for no-fault liability purposes, regardless of its mode of supply or usage.
rule_text_technical: Software, including operating systems, firmware, computer programs, applications or AI systems, constitutes a product for the purposes of no-fault liability, irrespective of whether it is stored on a device, accessed through a communication network or cloud technologies, or supplied through a software-as-a-service model; a developer or producer of software, including AI system providers within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, shall be treated as a manufacturer.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You cannot apply product liability rules to the content of digital files such as media files, e-books, or mere source code of software, as information is not considered a product.
rule_text_technical: Information is not to be considered a product, and product liability rules shall therefore not apply to the content of digital files, such as media files, e-books, or the mere source code of software.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You cannot apply this Directive to free and open-source software developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity, but you must apply it if such software is supplied in exchange for a price or for personal data used beyond improving security, compatibility, or interoperability.
rule_text_technical: This Directive shall not apply to free and open-source software developed or supplied outside the course of a commercial activity; however, where software is supplied in exchange for a price, or for personal data used other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software, and is therefore supplied in the course of a commercial activity, this Directive shall apply.

first_instance.law_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: If you integrate free and open-source software supplied outside a commercial activity into your product in the course of a commercial activity, you may be held liable for damage caused by the defectiveness of that software component.
rule_text_technical: Where free and open-source software supplied outside the course of a commercial activity is subsequently integrated by a manufacturer as a component into a product in the course of a commercial activity and is thereby placed on the market, it shall be possible to hold that manufacturer liable for damage caused by the defectiveness of such software; the original developer of the open-source software shall not be held liable as they would not have fulfilled the conditions of placing a product or component on the market.

rule_text: You must treat digital manufacturing files — which contain functional information to produce tangible items by enabling automated control of machinery — as products subject to product liability rules when developed or supplied in the course of a commercial activity.
rule_text_technical: Digital manufacturing files, which contain the functional information necessary to produce a tangible item by enabling the automated control of machinery or tools, such as drills, lathes, mills and 3D printers, shall be considered to be products for the purposes of no-fault liability where such files are developed or supplied in the course of a commercial activity.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU Product Liability Directive (2024) (European Union, 2024-11-18).

rule_text: You must treat digital services that are integrated into or interconnected with a product — such that their absence would prevent the product from performing one of its functions — as components of that product for product liability purposes, where those services are within the manufacturer's control.
rule_text_technical: Integrated or inter-connected digital services whose absence would prevent a product from performing one of its functions shall be considered components of the product into which they are integrated or with which they are inter-connected, where they are within the control of the manufacturer of that product, and shall therefore be subject to no-fault liability under this Directive.

rule_text: You are not required to disclose information in an explanation statement if doing so would unreasonably disclose the personal information of another individual or reveal commercially sensitive information or information that would prejudice law enforcement.
rule_text_technical: An APP entity is not required to include in an explanation statement information that would involve the unreasonable disclosure of personal information relating to another individual, or information that is commercially sensitive, or information the disclosure of which would be contrary to law enforcement interests.

rule_text: You must treat a decision as 'substantially automated' if it is made using an automated process and a human does not exercise meaningful deliberation or judgement in making the decision, even if a human nominally reviews or approves it.
rule_text_technical: A 'substantially automated decision' means a decision made using an automated process where a human being does not exercise meaningful deliberation or judgement in making the decision, and the fact that a human being nominally reviews or approves the decision does not of itself make the decision not substantially automated.

rule_text: You must treat a decision as having a 'significant effect' on an individual's rights or interests if it directly determines matters such as the individual's access to services, employment, credit, housing, education, or other matters prescribed by regulation.
rule_text_technical: A decision has a 'significant effect on the rights or interests of an individual' if it directly determines access to, or the terms and conditions of, goods or services, employment, credit, housing, education, legal proceedings, or other prescribed matters affecting the individual.

rule_text: The Minister must cause a review of the operation of the doxxing offence amendments in Schedule 3 to be commenced within two years of the Schedule 3 commencement date, and a report of that review must be tabled in each House of Parliament.
rule_text_technical: The Minister must cause a review of the operation of the amendments made by Schedule 3 to begin within 2 years after the commencement of that Schedule, and must cause a report of that review to be prepared and tabled in each House of the Parliament within 15 sitting days after the report is completed.

rule_text: You cannot publish or distribute personal information about an individual online with the intent to cause them physical or mental harm, harassment, or intimidation.
rule_text_technical: Schedule 3 inserts doxxing offences into the Criminal Code Act 1995 that prohibit the use of a carriage service to transmit, make available, publish, distribute, advertise or promote personal data of one or more individuals with the intention of causing physical or mental harm to, or harassing or intimidating, those individuals.

first_instance.law_name: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 — Automated Decision-Making Provisions

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Australia Privacy Act ADM Amendment (Australia, 2024-12-10).

Both prohibit publishing identifying information online likely to cause harassment or harm, but the Singapore rule focuses on a reasonable-person standard for intent and does not require proof of a protected characteristic, whereas the Australian rule requires intent to cause physical or mental harm.

instances.citation: Obligations for Generative AI Service Providers — Prohibition on Generating Certain Content, ¶1
instances.notes: Both prohibit harmful non-consensual content involving real individuals, but the India rule is specific to generative AI producing sexual or defamatory synthetic media, whereas the Australian rule covers online publication of personal information with intent to cause harm or harassment.

instances.citation: Turkish Penal Code Amendment — Art. 5237 (§ Deepfake Criminal Offence)
instances.notes: Both criminalize deliberate creation and distribution of content intended to harm another person's reputation or cause psychological harm, but Turkey's rule is specific to AI-generated deepfakes and includes enhanced penalties, while the Australian rule focuses on doxxing of personal information online.

rule_text: You cannot doxx individuals targeting them because of a protected characteristic such as race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, or disability; doing so constitutes an aggravated criminal offence.
rule_text_technical: Schedule 3 creates an aggravated doxxing offence under the Criminal Code Act 1995 where the conduct is motivated by the targeted individual's race, colour, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, intersex status, disability, nationality, national or ethnic origin, or religion.

rule_text: The Australian Information Commissioner has the power to conduct public inquiries into matters relating to automated decision-making and the privacy implications thereof, and APP entities must cooperate with such inquiries.
rule_text_technical: Schedule 1, Part 10 amends the Privacy Act 1988 to empower the Information Commissioner to conduct public inquiries into matters of public importance relating to privacy, which may include the use of personal information in substantially automated decisions, and imposes cooperation obligations on APP entities subject to inquiry.

rule_text: National and local government bodies must respect the creative spirit of AI business operators and work to create a safe environment for AI use.
rule_text_technical: National and local government bodies should respect the creative spirit of AI business operators and work to create a safe environment for AI use.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Korea AI Basic Act (South Korea, 2024-12-26).

rule_text: National and local government bodies should design policies that allow everyone to adapt smoothly to social, economic, cultural, and everyday-life changes brought about by AI.
rule_text_technical: National and local government bodies should design policies that allow everyone to adapt smoothly to the social, economic, cultural, and everyday-life changes brought about by AI.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Korea AI Basic Act (South Korea, 2024-12-26).

rule_text: The Minister of Science and ICT must establish, amend, and implement an AI basic plan every three years, subject to deliberation and resolution by the National AI Committee.
rule_text_technical: Every three years, the Minister of Science and ICT shall establish, amend, and implement an AI basic plan to promote AI technology and the AI industry and strengthen national competitiveness, subject to deliberation and resolution by the National AI Committee, covering specified mandatory content areas.

first_instance.law_name: Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust

instances.notes: Rule introduced in South Korea AI Basic Act (South Korea, 2024-12-26).

Both require a designated government body to develop and maintain a national AI strategy or plan, but the Argentine rule is a voluntary recommendation for the Secretariat of Digital Transformation while the Korean rule is a binding statutory mandate for the Minister of Science and ICT to establish a plan every three years.

instances.citation: AI Promotion Act (General Framework) — Institutional Establishment

rule_text: You must provide downstream providers with sufficient technical information about your GPAI model's capabilities and limitations to enable them to comply with their own obligations under the EU AI Act.
rule_text_technical: Providers placing GPAI models on the market must provide downstream providers with sufficient technical information, including information on the model's capabilities and limitations, to enable those downstream providers to comply with their own obligations under the EU AI Act.

instances.citation: Principle 2 — Appropriate Transparency and Explainability (regulator guidance — technical documentation)
instances.notes: Both address the requirement for developers to provide technical documentation to downstream parties, but the UK White Paper frames this as a soft recommendation for regulators to consider, whereas the EU GPAI guideline imposes a binding obligation on GPAI model providers.

Both require technical documentation enabling third-party assessment of AI systems, but the EU rule focuses on downstream provider information sharing for GPAI models while the Brazilian rule applies broadly to high-risk AI systems for conformity assessment purposes.

rule_text: You must report serious incidents relating to your GPAI model's operation across the EU to the EU AI Office within defined timeframes.
rule_text_technical: Providers of GPAI models (not designated as systemic-risk) must report serious incidents to the EU AI Office within defined timeframes where those incidents relate to the GPAI model's operation across the EU.

first_instance.law_name: European Commission Guidelines on the Scope of Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models (Article 53 EU AI Act)

instances.notes: Rule introduced in EU GPAI Guidelines (Art. 53) (European Union, 2025-07-18).

Both require reporting of serious incidents involving AI systems to a supervisory authority, but Brazil's rule targets high-risk AI systems reported to the ANPD with specific harm triggers (death, serious injury, fundamental rights), while the EU rule covers GPAI models reported to the EU AI Office with defined timeframes.

rule_text: Your GPAI model is presumed to pose systemic risk if it was trained using a total computing power exceeding 10²⁵ FLOPs, triggering enhanced obligations under Article 55.
rule_text_technical: A GPAI model is subject to a rebuttable presumption of systemic risk designation under Article 51 where it was trained using a total computing power exceeding 10²⁵ floating point operations (FLOPs); the Commission may also designate lower-threshold models as systemic risk based on number of users, cross-sectoral reach, or capability evaluations.

first_instance.law_name: European Commission Guidelines on the Scope of Obligations for Providers of General-Purpose AI Models (Article 53 EU AI Act)

rule_text: You must comply with Article 53 obligations if your GPAI model was trained using a total computing power exceeding 10²³ FLOPs, as established in Annex XIII of the EU AI Act.
rule_text_technical: The training compute threshold triggering Article 53 GPAI model obligations is 10²³ floating point operations (FLOPs), as established in Annex XIII of the EU AI Act and confirmed by these Guidelines.

rule_text: If your GPAI model is designated as posing systemic risk, you must assess and mitigate systemic risks including cascading effects, large-scale manipulation, and critical infrastructure disruption.
rule_text_technical: Providers of systemic-risk GPAI models must, pursuant to Article 55, assess and mitigate systemic risks including but not limited to cascading effects, large-scale manipulation, and critical infrastructure disruption.

rule_text: If you do not adhere to the GPAI Code of Practice, you must demonstrate compliance with Articles 53 and 55 obligations through alternative means.
rule_text_technical: Compliance with the GPAI Code of Practice developed under Article 56 creates a rebuttable presumption of conformity with Articles 53 and 55 obligations; providers that do not adhere to the Code must demonstrate compliance through alternative means.

rule_text: You may face a penalty of up to 3% of worldwide annual turnover or €15 million (whichever is higher) for failing to comply with Article 53 or Article 55 obligations as a GPAI model provider.
rule_text_technical: The maximum penalty for GPAI providers failing to comply with Article 53 or Article 55 obligations is up to 3% of worldwide annual turnover, subject to a minimum floor of €15 million for Article 53 obligations; the same maximum applies for Article 55 systemic-risk obligations.

instances.citation: Chapter V (Penalty Table — High-Risk AI Obligations)
instances.notes: Both rules establish a fine ceiling of €15,000,000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, but the existing rule targets GPAI model obligations (Articles 53/54) while this rule targets high-risk AI system obligations under the EU AI Act, representing a different substantive scope.

The penalty of up to €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover for GPAI provider obligation violations is verbatim transposition of the EU AI Act Article 99 GPAI tier, matching the existing rule exactly.

Both impose percentage-of-turnover fines for non-compliance, but the DSA sets a 6% cap for VLOPs/VLOSEs under platform obligations, whereas the GPAI guidelines set a 3% cap for GPAI model obligations under the EU AI Act framework, reflecting different regulatory instruments, subjects, and thresholds.

rule_text: You must recognise the Health and Safety Authority as the national competent authority for machinery and machinery products used in the workplace (Annex I, Section A, Point 1).
rule_text_technical: The Health and Safety Authority is designated as the market surveillance authority and national competent authority for the purposes of Article 70(1) in respect of Point 1 of Section A, Annex I of the Artificial Intelligence Regulation, as regards machinery and machinery products used in the workplace.

Both rules designate a financial sector authority (BaFin vs. Central Bank of Ireland) as the competent market surveillance authority for AI in financial services, but Germany's rule explicitly lists specific financial AI use cases and is framed as a binding sectoral jurisdiction rule under national implementing legislation.

rule_text: You must recognise the Data Protection Commission as the market surveillance authority for the purposes of Article 74(8) of the AI Regulation.

rule_text: You are not subject to the criminal prohibition under RSA 639:3 III-a(a) if you are a cloud service provider or a provider of a telecommunications or information service (as defined in 47 U.S.C. § 153) and the relevant content was created by or supplied on behalf of another person.
rule_text_technical: The criminal prohibition under RSA 639:3 III-a(a) shall not apply to a cloud service provider, or a provider of a telecommunications service or an information service as defined in 47 U.S.C. section 153, with respect to the provision of content created by or supplied on behalf of another person.

rule_text_technical: The criminal prohibition under RSA 639:3 III-a(a) shall not apply to any product, service, website, or application that provides an AI chat program or character that is integral or incidental to a video game, television, streaming, movie, or other similar interactive experience.

rule_text: You must not, as an owner or operator of an AI chat program, large language model bot, chatbot, character AI, or similar responsive generative communication application, knowingly direct communications to a child with the intent to facilitate, encourage, offer, solicit, or recommend that the child imminently engage in sexually explicit conduct, production of visual depictions of such conduct, illegal drug or alcohol use, self-harm or suicide, or violence against another person — violating this rule makes you civilly liable to the child, the child's parent, or next friend.
rule_text_technical: Any owner or operator of a computer online service, Internet service, or bulletin board service, including a provider of an AI chat program, large language model AI bot, chat bot, character AI, or other computer application whose sole purpose is to provide responsive open-ended generative communication through AI, shall be liable to a child, parent of such child, or next friend of such child if the owner or operator knows at the time they direct the communication to the child that the communication is made with the intent to facilitate, encourage, offer, solicit, or recommend that the child imminently engage in: (a) sexually explicit conduct; (b) the production or participation in the production of a visual depiction of such conduct; (c) the illegal use of drugs or alcohol; (d) acts of self-harm or suicide; or (e) any crime of violence against another person.

rule_text: You cannot use AI-generated imagery, voice synthesis, or biometric replication tools to create fraudulent identity documents, synthetic voice recordings, or digital likenesses; doing so aggravates the underlying falsification offense with increased imprisonment, fines, and disqualification from public office.
rule_text_technical: When the crimes of falsification of documents (Article 290) or use of falsified documents (Article 291) of Law 599 of 2000 are committed using AI-generated imagery, voice synthesis, or biometric replication tools to create fraudulent identity documents, synthetic voice recordings, or digital likenesses, the following enhanced penalties apply: (i) imprisonment range increases by one-third; (ii) monetary fine increases by one-half; (iii) the defendant is prohibited from holding public office for a period equal to twice the imprisonment sentence.

rule_text_technical: Under new Article 218A of Law 599 of 2000, the causing of severe psychological harm to the victim constitutes an aggravating circumstance for the offense of non-consensual dissemination of AI-generated intimate imagery.

rule_text: You cannot use AI-generated voice cloning, facial synthesis (deepfakes), or automated impersonation tools to deceive victims into making financial transfers or disclosing credentials; doing so aggravates the electronic fraud offense with imprisonment of 48 to 108 months and fines of 200 to 1,500 minimum wages.
rule_text_technical: The crime of electronic fraud under Article 269I of Law 599 of 2000 is specifically aggravated when AI-generated voice cloning, facial synthesis (deepfakes), or automated impersonation tools are used to deceive victims into financial transfers or disclosure of credentials; enhanced penalties are imprisonment of 48 to 108 months (increased from 36 to 72 months) and a fine of 200 to 1,500 minimum wages (increased from 100 to 1,000 minimum wages).

rule_text: If you are a micro-enterprise as defined in Law No. 28015, you are subject to simplified compliance procedures rather than full compliance obligations.
rule_text_technical: Micro-enterprises as defined in Law No. 28015 and its amendments are subject to simplified compliance procedures as set out in Chapter VII of these Regulations, in lieu of standard compliance requirements.

rule_text_technical: The National Secretariat of Digital Government (SNGD) of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers is designated as the lead competent authority for the implementation, supervision, and enforcement of these Regulations and Law No. 31814, in coordination with sectoral regulators.

rule_text: The SNGD must coordinate with sectoral regulators on AI governance in regulated sectors.
rule_text_technical: The SNGD shall coordinate with sectoral regulators on AI governance in regulated sectors, ensuring coherent supervisory oversight.

rule_text: Your AI system is classified as high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of critical infrastructure, including energy, water, and transportation systems, or is itself critical infrastructure.
rule_text_technical: An AI system is classified as high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of critical infrastructure, including energy, water, and transportation systems, or is the critical infrastructure itself.

first_instance.law_name: Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM — Implementing Regulations for Law 31814 on Responsible Use of AI

instances.notes: Rule introduced in Peru AI Implementing Regulation (SD 115-2025) (Peru, 2025-09-09).

Both laws establish tiered risk classification for AI systems based on impact on safety and rights, but Kazakhstan uses a three-tier structure (minimum, medium, high) while Peru's regulation defines high-risk categories by specific use-case domains without an explicit lower tier.

Both establish tiered/categorical AI risk classification, but Vietnam uses a three-tier system (high/medium/low) defined by potential damage criteria, whereas Peru's rules enumerate specific high-risk use-case categories without a formal three-tier structure.

Both classify or categorize AI systems based on their potential impact on critical infrastructure safety and security to guide risk management prioritization, but the DHS rule is a voluntary guidance instrument recommending categorization, while the Peru regulation is a binding classification mandate.

rule_text: Your AI system is classified as high-risk if it is used by or on behalf of law enforcement to assess crime risk, conduct polygraph-like testing, evaluate evidence reliability, assess reoffending risk, or profile persons.
rule_text_technical: An AI system is classified as high-risk if it is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities to assess the risk of individuals committing crimes, to carry out polygraph testing or similar tools, to evaluate the reliability of evidence, to assess the risk of reoffending, or to profile persons.

first_instance.law_name: Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM — Implementing Regulations for Law 31814 on Responsible Use of AI

rule_text: Your AI system is classified as high-risk if it is used in immigration, asylum, and border control management, including risk assessment, identity verification, examination of asylum applications, or entry decisions.
rule_text_technical: An AI system is classified as high-risk if it is used in immigration, asylum, and border control management, including risk assessment of persons, verification of identity, examination of asylum applications, or decisions on entry.

rule_text: Your AI system is classified as high-risk if it is used in the administration of justice, including assisting judicial authorities in researching or interpreting facts, law, or applying legal norms to specific cases.
rule_text_technical: An AI system is classified as high-risk if it is used in the administration of justice, including assisting judicial authorities in researching and interpreting facts and law and in applying legal norms to specific cases.

rule_text: Your AI system is classified as high-risk if it is used in democratic processes, including electoral systems and campaign targeting.
rule_text_technical: An AI system is classified as high-risk if it is used in democratic processes, including electoral systems and campaign targeting.

rule_text: The SNGD may update the list of high-risk AI system categories by administrative resolution following public consultation, and must publish updates in the Official Gazette.
rule_text_technical: The SNGD may update the list of high-risk AI system categories and subcategories in Annex I by administrative resolution, following public consultation, to reflect technological and market developments and emerging risks; updates shall be published in the Official Gazette.

Both rules define criteria or procedures for determining risk classification levels, but Vietnam specifies substantive criteria (human rights impact, field of use, autonomy level, scale) while Peru's rule focuses on the administrative update mechanism for the high-risk list.

Both rules address the process of developing legal/regulatory requirements for AI classification by assessing risk factors, but the Russian rule broadly covers the criteria (purpose, probability, scale of harm) for developing legal regulations generally, while the Peruvian rule focuses on administrative updating of a specific high-risk category list.

rule_text: Your conformity assessment must verify that the AI system meets the applicable technical requirements set out in Article 9.
rule_text_technical: The conformity assessment shall cover verification that the AI system meets the applicable technical requirements set out in Article 9 of these Regulations.

rule_text: You must retain conformity assessment documentation for ten years after the system is placed on the market and make it available to the SNGD upon request.
rule_text_technical: Providers shall retain conformity assessment documentation for ten years after the system is placed on the market and shall make it available to the SNGD upon request.

rule_text: You must maintain a protocol for preventing the production of suicidal ideation, suicide, or self-harm content to users, including providing crisis service provider referrals when a user expresses such content, before allowing a companion chatbot to engage with users on your platform.

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California SB 243 (Companion Chatbot) (California, 2025-10-13).

Both require a protocol for preventing/addressing suicidal ideation content in AI chatbot contexts, but the Washington rule is scoped specifically to AI companion chatbots and focuses on detection and addressing, while the California rule covers a broader range of AI products and also explicitly includes crisis service referrals in the main obligation.

Both require a protocol for preventing suicidal/self-harm content and providing crisis resources, but Oregon's rule emphasizes detection of ideation/intent while California's frames it as preventing production of such content.

instances.notes: Both rules require conversational/interactive AI systems to maintain protocols preventing harmful self-harm/suicidal content and providing crisis resources, but Iowa SF 2417 focuses on recognition mechanisms within the protocol while California SB 243 emphasizes preventing production of such content and providing crisis services.

rule_text: You must, by default, provide a clear and conspicuous notification to any user you know is a minor at least every three hours during continuing companion chatbot interactions, reminding the user to take a break and that the chatbot is artificially generated and not human.
rule_text_technical: An operator shall, for a user that the operator knows is a minor, provide by default a clear and conspicuous notification to the user at least every three hours for continuing companion chatbot interactions that reminds the user to take a break and that the companion chatbot is artificially generated and not human.

first_instance.law_name: Companion Chatbot Safety and Disclosure Act

instances.notes: Rule introduced in California SB 243 (Companion Chatbot) (California, 2025-10-13).

Both require repeated AI disclosure notifications every three hours during continued interaction for general users, but Washington's rule applies to all users of AI companion chatbots while California's rule specifically targets users known to be minors.

Both address disclosure obligations specifically toward minor users interacting with AI systems, but Idaho requires a persistent or visible AI identity disclosure for minor account holders while California requires a recurring notification at least every three hours during companion AI sessions.

Both impose heightened disclosure obligations when interacting with minor users of AI companion platforms, but Oregon's rule requires specified statements and disclosures upon detecting a minor whereas California's rule mandates periodic notifications every three hours during continuing companion interactions.

Both require persistent or repeated AI identity disclosure specifically for minor users, but Iowa SF 2417 mandates continuous visibility of AI identity throughout the interaction while California SB 243 requires a notification at least every three hours, representing a meaningful difference in the standard and mechanism.

rule_text: You cannot communicate online material that a reasonable person would conclude is threatening, abusive, insulting, sexual or indecent and is likely to cause a person harassment, alarm, distress or humiliation.

Both rules impose civil penalties per violation against regulated entities for AI-related statutory non-compliance, but Idaho's rule adds injunctive relief, sets a higher per-violation amount ($1,000) with a $500,000 aggregate cap per operator, and allows actual damages as an alternative, while Indiana's rule caps at $1,000 per violation with no stated aggregate cap and no injunction or actual damages provision.

Both impose civil penalties for healthcare AI chatbot violations, but Tennessee uses a tiered escalating structure ($5,000/$25,000/$50,000) covering first, second, and subsequent violations, whereas Indiana's law imposes a flat $1,000 per violation for payment assistance notice non-compliance, resulting in meaningfully different thresholds and penalty structures.
